archetypes.label: Hungry Assistant Prof
archetypes.tagline: New to the job and hungry for papers.

archetypes.label: Kind but Unfunded
archetypes.tagline: Fights for their students on almost no budget.

archetypes.label: Grant Machine
archetypes.tagline: Never short of funding, or of grant reports to write.

archetypes.label: The Visionary
archetypes.tagline: Big ideas, and a new one every week.

archetypes.label: Near Retirement

fixed_quirks: Meticulous about layout and visual detail: orphan words, consistent capitalization, figure fonts.
Always finds the major flaw, and asks the hard but critical question.
Replies at strange hours, midnight included, always adding "no need to reply until Monday".
Buys bubble tea for everyone who comes to lab meeting in person.

quirks: Replies to email at 3 am.
Loves Gantt charts.
Always wants "just one more experiment".
Draws everything on a whiteboard.
Forgets meetings, then remembers them better than you do.
Sends papers with no message, only the PDF.
Writes "great!!" on everything and means it 40% of the time.
Insists on tables over figures.
Only meets while walking.
Seems to know every reviewer personally.
Has a favorite font and enforces it.
Plays devil's advocate even when agreeing with you.
Answers questions with questions.
Remembers every student's birthday.
Brings snacks to lab meeting.
Says "let's write a grant about it" about everything.
Keeps a list of every idea anyone has ever had in lab meeting.
Takes calls from the car, always slightly out of signal.
Prefers a 2-hour meeting to a 2-line email.
Has strong opinions about the Oxford comma.
Quotes papers from the 1990s from memory.
Reads drafts on paper, with a red pen.
Schedules meetings in 25-minute blocks.
Responds to long emails with a single emoji.
Keeps a plant in the lab that nobody else may water.
Always asks "what's the one-sentence version?"
Starts every meeting with "so, what did we learn this week?"
Has a standing Friday-afternoon reading group nobody can escape.

endings.name: Tenure-Track Professor
endings.offer: An assistant professor job: your own lab, and your own grant rejections.
endings.text: You start your own lab. Your first student arrives in September, nervous and brilliant. You catch yourself saying things your advisor used to say, and you mostly mean them.

endings.name: Professor at a Teaching College
endings.offer: A teaching job with small classes and students who come to office hours.
endings.text: You teach, and you are good at it. Every year a few students find you after class with a question that turns into a project.

endings.name: Postdoc in a Famous Lab
endings.offer: Two years in a lab everyone has heard of.
endings.text: You join a lab whose papers you used to read in reading group. The coffee is better and the deadlines are the same.

endings.name: The Eternal Postdoc
endings.offer: A postdoc, and probably another one after that.
endings.text: Your first postdoc becomes your second. You know every visa form by heart and every reviewer by writing style.

endings.name: Lecturer Across the Pond
endings.offer: A permanent lectureship overseas, with a new vocabulary for everything.
endings.text: You move abroad, learn what "REF" means, and find that most collaborations start at the tea break.

endings.name: Faculty Back Home
endings.offer: A faculty job in your home country, near family.
endings.text: You go home with a doctorate and a suitcase of ideas. Your parents finally understand your job: you are a professor now.

endings.name: Research Scientist at a Frontier Lab
endings.offer: A research job at one of the labs everyone is racing.
endings.text: You join a frontier lab with more compute than you can imagine. Sometimes your name is on a paper the whole field reads.

endings.name: Research Scientist at Big Tech
endings.offer: A research scientist role with a stable team and a nice badge.
endings.text: You become a research scientist at a big company. You still publish, but now there's a budget and nobody asks you to TA.

endings.name: Applied Scientist
endings.offer: Build models that real users touch.
endings.text: Your models ship. Millions of people use something you made, and none of them know your name, which turns out to be fine.

endings.name: ML Engineer (with a PhD, for Fun)
endings.offer: Good pay, and coworkers who call you Doctor as a joke.
endings.text: You write code all day and sleep well at night. Sometimes you miss research. Then someone mentions Reviewer 2, and you stop missing it.

endings.name: Quant Researcher
endings.offer: A trading firm wants your statistics skills.
endings.text: You move into finance. The salary is absurd, and your p-values are finally worth money.

endings.name: UX Researcher
endings.offer: Lead user research for AI products.
endings.text: You spend your days talking to the people who use AI products, which is what your PhD trained you to do best. Product teams start asking for you by name.

endings.name: The Return Offer
endings.offer: Your internship team wants you back, full time.
endings.text: You go back to the team from your internship. Your old desk is still there, and so is the sticky note you left on the monitor.

endings.name: Founder, Acquired
endings.text: You start a company from your thesis. Three stressful years later, a big company buys it. You take a long vacation, then start reading papers again.

endings.name: Founder, Pivoted to B2B SaaS
endings.text: Your startup begins as a research vision and becomes a dashboard for enterprise customers. It pays the bills. You still have the original slide deck.

endings.name: Founder, Then Big Tech
endings.text: Your startup doesn't make it, and you learn more in eighteen months than in five years of grad school. A big lab hires you the week after you close it.

endings.name: Start Your Own Company
endings.offer: Turn your thesis into a startup. The risk is high and the stories are great.

endings.name: Employee #4 at a Labmate's Startup
endings.offer: Your old labmate's startup wants you, and it's offering equity and chaos.
endings.text: You join your labmate's startup as employee number four. The office is a converted garage and the whiteboard has your old lab's handwriting on it.

endings.name: Policy Fellow
endings.offer: A fellowship advising on AI policy.
endings.text: You explain language models to people who write the rules. Then you explain them again the next week.

endings.name: Science Journalist
endings.offer: Write about AI for people who will never read an arXiv paper.
endings.text: You become the person who explains AI research to the public, carefully, without the hype. Researchers start sending you their preprints.

endings.name: AI YouTuber
endings.offer: Your paper explainer videos have an audience. Make it a job.
endings.text: Your paper explainers find an audience and a sponsor. The comments are full of grad students thanking you.

endings.name: Clinical Informatics at a Hospital
endings.offer: Join a hospital's informatics team and put your work at the bedside.
endings.text: You join the hospital you used to recruit clinicians from. Now you're the one they call when the alerts don't make sense, and you fix them.

endings.name: Master's Out, Happily
endings.text: You leave with a Master's degree and no regrets. The skills come with you, and so do the friends.

endings.name: Bubble Tea Shop Owner
endings.text: You open a bubble tea shop near campus. Grad students come in at odd hours, and you always know what they need: half sugar, and someone to say the paper will be fine.

endings.name: Switched Fields
endings.text: You start medical school. Your classmates are amazed that you already know what an EHR is, and that you have opinions about its interface.

endings.name: Back to the Family Business
endings.text: You go home and join the family business. Within a year you've automated the inventory and your aunt calls you "the scientist".

endings.name: The Eternal Student
endings.text: Year eight ends and the university gently points out the time limit. You leave with a Master's degree and a drawer of almost-finished papers.

epilogues.text: You and your partner still argue about whose thesis acknowledgments were sweeter.
Your cat still sleeps on the keyboard. Some of your best emails were typed by paw.
You kept exercising, and your back still works.
You pulled too many all-nighters in grad school. Now you go to bed at ten.
Your friends from grad school are still your closest friends.
Your family framed your diploma before you did.
You and your advisor still meet for coffee when you're in town.
You buy bubble tea for your own team when they come in person, just like your advisor did.
You notice orphan words everywhere now, even on wedding invitations.
Your first first-author paper is still the one you're proudest of.
You keep a folder of every rejection. It's thicker than your CV.
Somewhere, a first-year is reading your paper in reading group and loving it.
You saw more of the world through conferences than in the rest of your life combined.
You still play music on weekends, and you're better at it than ever.
The clinicians you worked with still send you interesting problems.
You mentor a few students informally. You tell them to close the laptop sometimes.
You learned to say no, which was the hardest skill the PhD taught you.

flavor.text: You open final_v3_REAL_final.tex.
The coffee machine breaks. Lab productivity falls by a third.
The building's heating is either off or set to Sahara.
Your experiment finishes. It was the wrong config.
The printer jams the morning of your poster session.
An undergrad calls you "professor". You don't correct them.
You accidentally reply-all to the department list.
Your virtual background slips during a job interview. Your laundry makes a brief appearance.
The fire alarm goes off during your practice talk.
A "quick sync" is booked for 90 minutes.
A package update breaks your Python environment.
An hour-long bug turns out to be a typo in a config key.
You find your own paper on a course reading list, described wrongly.
"Can you hear me?" Four times, at the start of every meeting.
Your paper gets cited for the opposite of what it says.
Orientation week. The new students still believe the GPU queue is a myth.
Fall semester starts. The lab fridge still holds three yogurts from last spring.
Three people at the department Halloween party come dressed as chatbots.
The lab is empty for Thanksgiving week. The GPUs are all yours.
Finals week. The library has no free seats and one working outlet.
You grade the same wrong answer 43 times.
Office hours before the midterm. The line reaches the elevator.
Winter break. The building is quiet, and the heating has gone home too.
Your out-of-office reply says you're on break. You answer emails anyway.
New semester, new to-do list. It looks a lot like the old one.
It's dark by 4:30 pm. Your body clock files a complaint.
The lab group chat fills with red envelope emojis.
Spring break. The undergrads leave, and the campus Wi-Fi finally works.
The trees outside the lab bloom. You admire them through the window.
Regrade requests arrive, all sent after midnight.
Annual review season. You list your accomplishments, then add some stronger verbs.
Summer starts. The campus is quiet and the parking is easy.
Half the lab is on internships. Lab meeting is three people and a laptop.
The building's AC gives up in the heat wave. The server room is the coolest place on campus.
The new cohort arrives. They all have better laptops than you.
The lab chat gains eleven new members, and eleven new questions about the cluster.
Half the lab is coughing. The other half is wearing masks and looking worried.
Someone microwaves fish in the lab kitchen again.
Lab meeting runs 40 minutes over. Nobody knows why.
The lab fridge has a sign that says "Please label your food". The sign is not labeled.
A labmate brings homemade cookies. Productivity rises briefly, then falls.
Someone renames the lab Wi-Fi to "Reviewer2_Is_Watching".
The most senior student in the lab tells a deadline story with three morals.
You find a comment in the lab codebase that just says "sorry".
The group chat debates lunch for an hour. Everyone eats at their desk.
The GPU queue has 412 jobs ahead of yours. You read a paper instead.
Your loss curve goes down smoothly. You don't trust it.
You spend an hour making a figure colorblind-friendly. It also prints better now.
Your random seed is 42, like everyone else's.
Your experiment log says "try again tomorrow". It was written three weeks ago.
A bug in your evaluation script makes your results worse and more honest.
Overleaf reports 37 errors. The PDF looks fine.
You rename a file from results to results_new to results_final to results_final2.
Your notes from last month say "KEY INSIGHT" with nothing after it.
The paper you need is behind a paywall. Your university has access, but your VPN doesn't.
A tokenizer splits your name into five pieces.
Your model answers every question with a confident paragraph about penguins.
Your prompt is now longer than your abstract.
Someone at lab meeting says "just fine-tune it" as if it's one step.
Your baseline gets better after you fix a bug. Your method doesn't.
You read a paper that solves your problem. It's from 1998.
A related-work search for your topic returns your own paper first.
Your job crashes at 98%.
Your annotation guidelines are now 14 pages long. Nobody agrees on what counts as "neutral".
Inter-annotator agreement comes back at 0.41. You learn the word "moderate".
You compute Cohen's kappa three times and get three different numbers.
A study participant asks whether the chatbot in your study is a real person.
Your think-aloud participant thinks very quietly.
A participant rates your prototype 7 out of 7, then says they never clicked it.
A pilot participant finds the bug you hunted all week. It takes them four seconds.
The anchor on your survey scale says "Strongly Disagre". It's been live for a day.
Your interview transcript has 40 instances of "um". Thirty-eight are yours.
The IRB asks you to change "may" to "might" on page 12.
A clinician partner replies to a three-paragraph email with one word: "Thursday?"
A participant stays after the session to tell you how to fix your whole interface. They're right.
You spend an afternoon choosing between "utilize" and "use". You choose "use".
You now notice orphan words in other people's papers.
Your abstract is 251 words. The limit is 250.
Your bibliography has the same paper three times, with three different years.
You move a figure up one line. LaTeX moves it two pages down.
Your paper title has a colon, like every other title on the reading list.
You write "Interestingly," and then delete it. Then you write it again.
Your conference badge spells your name wrong. You answer to it all week.
The line for coffee is longer than the line for the keynote.
You come home with four tote bags and no memory of picking them up.
Everyone at your poster asks the same question. You start answering before they finish.
You meet someone whose papers you've cited six times. You forget their name instantly.
Your advisor replies at 12:40 am: "Great figure. No need to reply until Monday."
Your advisor buys bubble tea for everyone who came to lab meeting in person.
Your advisor spots an orphan word on page 6 of your draft.
Your advisor answers your email from a different airport than last week.
Your advisor schedules a check-in about your check-in.
Your advisor has a new grant and, with it, a new spreadsheet.
Your advisor pitches a startup idea over lunch. It's the third one this month.
Your advisor asks whether your p-value survived the correction.
Your advisor tells a story from 1994 that turns out to be exactly relevant.
Your advisor sketches a ten-year research vision on a napkin.
Your advisor sends you a paper at 6 am with the subject line "!!".
Your advisor apologizes that the travel budget is, once again, mostly hope.
Your advisor forwards a message from the company side with one word: "thoughts?"
Your cat sits on the exact paragraph you're reading.
Your cat knocks your coffee off the desk, then looks at you.
The lab whiteboard still has equations from 2019. Nobody dares erase them.
Your citation profile gets merged with someone who has a similar name. You now have three papers on dairy cattle.
A squirrel outside the window becomes the lab mascot. It now has its own channel in the lab chat.
The vending machine eats your last dollar. The granola bar hangs there, just out of reach.
You name your model after a faction from your favorite sci-fi novel. The reviewers don't get the reference.

flavor_advisor.text: Your advisor's out-of-office reply has its own out-of-office reply.
You catch your advisor on a conference livestream. It's the longest you've seen them this month.
A calendar invite arrives: "Sync about the sync."
Your advisor leaves a comment on your comment.
Your advisor's whiteboard says "Papers this year: 9", and it's only October.
The lab's one GPU has a sign-up sheet taped to it. Your advisor always signs up last.
Every slide at lab meeting now has an Aim number in the corner.
Your advisor's new idea arrived at 2 am. By 9 am it had a sequel.
Your advisor joins lab meeting from a company building, in front of a ping-pong table.
Your advisor starts a sentence with "Back in 1994". You take notes.
Your advisor's email signature lists four companies. One is new this week.
Your advisor writes "n = ?" in the margin of your vacation request.
Your advisor replies at 1:12 am: "Great figure."
You now notice orphan words in other people's papers.
Lab meeting bubble tea arrives. Yours is already labeled.
Your advisor fixes the capitalization in your email's subject line.
A comment on your draft asks "Who cares?", followed by a small smiley face.

opportunities.label: Go home for the holidays
opportunities.reason: The holidays are here. Everyone else is leaving campus.
opportunities.text: You eat home cooking and see old friends. Only one relative asks about your h-index.

opportunities.label: Take the winter break off
opportunities.reason: Winter break. The lab is empty and the inbox is quiet.
opportunities.text: You take a real break and start the new year with a clear head.

opportunities.label: Celebrate Lunar New Year
opportunities.reason: Lunar New Year is here, and the family group chat is busy.
opportunities.text: You eat too many dumplings and call everyone back home.

opportunities.label: Take a spring break trip
opportunities.reason: Spring break. Friends are planning a trip somewhere warm.
opportunities.text: You spend a week in the sun without reading a single paper.

opportunities.label: Take a real vacation
opportunities.reason: It's summer, and you haven't taken more than a weekend off in a long time.
opportunities.text: Two weeks without a laptop. It feels strange for two days, then wonderful.

opportunities.label: Go to a summer school
opportunities.reason: A summer school on human-centered NLP has a spot for you.
opportunities.text: You hear lectures from people whose papers you've read and join a group chat that lasts for years.

opportunities.label: Join a hackathon
opportunities.reason: A week-long hackathon on AI for health is looking for teammates.
opportunities.text: You barely sleep for a week. The demo works, and three teammates want to keep going.

opportunities.label: Join the writing retreat for “{project}”
opportunities.reason: The department's writing retreat has a seat open, in a quiet room with no meetings.
opportunities.text: Five quiet days later, the draft has grown more than it did all month.

opportunities.label: Run everything on the empty GPU cluster
opportunities.reason: Everyone else is at a conference. The GPU cluster is completely empty.
opportunities.text: With no queue, you run a month of experiments in a week.

opportunities.label: Run study sessions while the clinic has openings
opportunities.reason: The clinic suddenly has two weeks of open slots for your study.
opportunities.text: You run back-to-back sessions, and the clinicians all show up.

opportunities.label: Work side by side with your advisor
opportunities.reason: Your advisor's calendar is unexpectedly free for the next two weeks.
opportunities.text: You spend two weeks at the whiteboard with your advisor and learn how they think.

opportunities.label: Visit a collaborator's lab for two weeks
opportunities.reason: A collaborator invites you to spend two weeks in their lab.
opportunities.text: Their lab does things differently, and they spot problems you had stopped seeing.

opportunities.label: Help {labmate} make their deadline
opportunities.reason: {labmate} has a deadline Friday and is drowning.
opportunities.text: You fix the plots and rewrite the related work. They promise to return the favor.

opportunities.label: Take an undergrad under your wing
opportunities.reason: An eager undergrad wants to do research and your advisor suggests you.
opportunities.text: You spend two weeks setting them up, and explaining your work helps you understand it better.

opportunities.label: Prepare for the career fair
opportunities.reason: The fall career fair is next week. Recruiters from big labs will be there.
opportunities.text: You polish your CV and pitch, and come home with a tote bag of stickers.

opportunities.label: Give an invited talk at another university
opportunities.reason: A professor who read your paper invites you to give a talk.
opportunities.text: Your talk goes well, and the hard questions come from people who actually read the paper.

opportunities.label: Run a reading sprint with the lab
opportunities.reason: The lab wants to read the ten most important papers of the year, together, over the next two weeks.
opportunities.text: Ten papers and five arguments later, the lab roughly agrees on where the field is going.

opportunities.label: Teach the next two weeks of lectures
opportunities.reason: The professor you TA for is traveling and asks you to teach.
opportunities.text: You give three lectures, and your slides improve each time.

opportunities.label: Host prospective students at visit day
opportunities.reason: Visit day is coming. Your advisor asks you to show prospective students around.
opportunities.text: You hear yourself giving the advice you needed in your first year.

opportunities.label: Take two quiet weeks
opportunities.reason: You've been running on empty. Your advisor tells you to take some time.
opportunities.text: Nothing urgent turns out to be urgent. You come back steadier.

opportunities.label: Join the thesis-writing bootcamp
opportunities.reason: The graduate school runs a week-long thesis bootcamp.
opportunities.text: You write eight hours a day next to people doing the same. By Friday you have a chapter.

questions.text: Tell us about the classic paper on your list that everyone cites and nobody reads. What did it actually claim?
Why does self-attention get so expensive on long inputs, and what do people do about it?
What do word-overlap metrics like BLEU actually measure, and when do they disagree with people?
Can you average Likert responses and run a t-test on them? Defend your answer.
When would you choose a within-subjects design over a between-subjects one?
Explain subword tokenization. What goes wrong for languages it wasn't built for?
Your annotators reach a kappa of 0.4. Is that good? Who gets to decide?
If the whole field tunes on the same benchmark for five years, what are we actually measuring?
Your reading list is almost all NLP. What do you know about how HCI evaluates systems?
What can a think-aloud study tell you that a usage log cannot?
Ten years from now, which part of today's NLP will look naive?
Does a model that predicts the next word understand anything? Yes or no.
Explain how models are tuned with human preference feedback, and one way it can go wrong.
What exactly does a p-value of 0.04 tell you? And what doesn't it tell you?
Name two ways the wording of a survey question can bias the answer.
Which paper on your reading list do you disagree with most, and why?
You've read 80 papers. Which open problem in them do you think nobody is working on?
Why is this a PhD and not a product?
State your research question in one sentence. Now say it again without the word "LLM".
Who exactly benefits if this works, and have you asked them?
This looks like three PhDs. Which part would you cut?
Your timeline assumes IRB approval in four weeks. What happens if it takes twelve?
Twelve clinicians. How do you know that's enough?
What's the strongest baseline you are not planning to compare against?
If next year's model solves your task zero-shot, what is left of this thesis?
How do your three studies connect? Draw it for us.
How will you know your system helps people, beyond scoring well on a benchmark?
Does this scale?
What could go wrong for a participant in your study, and how will you prevent it?
Last year there were a dozen papers on LLM explanations for clinicians. How is yours different?
Your plan depends on hospital data you don't have yet. What's plan B?
What is the theoretical contribution here, beyond "we built it and people liked it"?
Who annotates your data, and how will you know they agree for the right reasons?
In one sentence: what does the field know now that it didn't before your thesis?
If you started your PhD again today, what would you do differently?
What is the biggest limitation of your thesis that no reviewer caught?
All your studies were in one hospital system. Why should anyone believe this generalizes?
In Chapter 3 you ran 14 tests on 20 participants. Did you correct for multiple comparisons?
Chapter 2 says users want more explanation. Chapter 4 says they ignored it. Which is it?
You used an LLM to grade your outputs. Who graded the grader?
Walk us through how your annotation guidelines changed between version 1 and the final version.
Could you explain Figure 5 again? Slowly, this time.
What is the first paper someone should write after reading your thesis?
Which result surprised you most, and did you believe it at first?
Could a new student reproduce your main result from the code you released?
Your title says "trustworthy". Did you measure trust, or did you ask people whether they trusted it?
Your main results use a model behind an API that has changed since. Are your numbers still valid?
Is this an NLP thesis or an HCI thesis? Pick one.
What will your lab be working on five years from now?
Who would fund this work, and what is your first grant proposal about?
What course would you teach here that we don't already offer?
Industry labs have a thousand times your compute. Why do this research at a university?
How is your research agenda different from your advisor's?
Who in this department would you collaborate with first, and on what?
How would you mentor a student who wants to work on something you don't know well?
Most of your citations come from one paper. What is your second act?
Has anyone actually used your system outside a study?
How would you evaluate an AI feature before it ships to millions of users?
Your topic is hot right now. What happens to your agenda when it cools down?
Why do you want to be here, specifically?
Your system is mostly prompts. What is the engineering contribution?
If we made you an offer and so did a big tech company, which would you take? Be honest.
Tell us about a time a class you taught went badly. What did you change?

recommendations.why: You burned out at least once.
You spent a lot of weekends working.
You rarely took real breaks.

tips.text: Classes have answers in the back of the book. Research doesn't, so the sooner you stop looking for them, the better.
Ask yourself why you're here, and be more honest than your statement of purpose was.
A harsh review is a free lesson from someone who read your paper closely. It just doesn't feel free.
If citations are the only thing keeping you going, you'll run dry. Find what you'd do even if nobody cited it.
The degree is just the receipt for what you actually bought: the training.

tips.topic: Hold Yourself to a High Standard
tips.text: Don't aim for borderline. Borderline is a coin flip with extra steps.
Whatever you promised in that rebuttal, do it. People remember who delivers.
Stop counting other people's papers. You aren't running the same race.
When you get stuck, learn the method behind the fix. You'll be stuck again.
Everyone starts strong. The middle years are the hard part, so pace yourself to finish.

tips.topic: Find Out What You Are Devoted To
tips.text: At some point it stops being your advisor's agenda. Make sure it becomes yours.
Snowball from one great paper: what it cites, and what cites it. Two hours of that beats a week of keyword searching.
Not every paper deserves a full read. Learn which ones do.
To learn a method, pick a paper you admire and work out how they did it.
Walk into advisor meetings with answers, and walk out with better ones.
If you can delete a paragraph and nothing breaks, delete it.
Write for a tired reviewer who is reading your paper fourth today.
Before you start a project, try answering ten hard questions about it. The ones you can't answer show you where to start.
If you can't state your research question in one sentence, you don't have one yet.
Who cares, and what has already been done? Answer those two and the introduction writes itself.
Your method should follow from the gap. If it doesn't, one of them is wrong.
Watch what people actually do between the clicks. That's where the design problems are.
A result is a number. A finding says what the number means, and that's what reviewers want.
Pick the venue whose readers will care most, not the one with the nicest logo.
Burnout builds up slowly, one skipped weekend at a time.
Your limits change every year of the PhD, so check them again.
Closing the laptop doesn't count as rest if you're still thinking about work.
You only have a few real hours of deep focus a day. Spend them on the hard part.

advisor.title: Quick Question
text: At 11:04 pm, {advisor} sends an email with the subject line "quick question". The question is not quick.
Your phone buzzes at 11 pm: "Quick question: could you rerun everything with the new data split?"

choices.label: Answer it tonight
choices.text: You reply at 12:40 am, and {advisor} answers "thx" at 12:41, which from them is high praise.

choices.label: Reply in the morning
choices.text: You sleep. By morning, a second email from {advisor} has answered the first one.

success.text: A thumbs-up comes back, and everyone gets to sleep.

failure.text: Two more "quick" emails arrive before midnight. You read them all.

advisor.title: Due Friday
text: {advisor} needs help with a grant proposal due Friday. "Just the preliminary results section. You know the work best."

choices.label: Write the section
choices.text: You write four pages about your own work in the future tense. {advisor} is clearly grateful.

choices.label: Offer figures, not prose
choices.text: You send two clean figures. Both end up on page one.

choices.label: Say your own deadline comes first

success.text: "Fair. Your paper matters more right now." You get your week back.

failure.text: {advisor} says "fine" in a way that is not quite fine.

advisor.title: A Brand-New Idea
text: {advisor} bursts into lab meeting with an exciting new idea. It's the idea you pitched last year, the one they called "not quite there".

success.text: {advisor} checks their notes and laughs. "Then you should lead it."

failure.text: "Similar, but this version is different." It is not different.

choices.label: Say "Great idea!" and smile
choices.text: You start a new folder for it. Your notes from last year are already inside.

choices.label: Send them your old slides
choices.text: "Ha, you were early." Your slides from last year become the starting point.

advisor.title: Rescheduled Into Your Vacation
text: {advisor} forgets your meeting and, to make up for it, moves it to the one week you'll be away.

choices.label: Take the call from vacation
choices.text: You take the 12-minute call from a parking lot, and {advisor} seems pleased.

success.text: "Oh! Of course. Enjoy your break." It moves to the week after.

failure.text: It moves to the morning you fly back.

choices.label: Send a written update instead
choices.text: You send a tidy one-page update. {advisor} replies "perfect, enjoy!" and means it.

advisor.title: Tomorrow's Guest Lecture
text: {advisor} is stuck in another meeting. "Could you give my guest lecture tomorrow? The slides are mostly done."

success.text: The slides are from 2019, but you narrate them well. Two students ask for your email.

failure.text: Slide 14 cites a model nobody has heard of. You improvise for ten long minutes.

choices.label: Rebuild the slides tonight
choices.text: You give a crisp lecture built around your own work. {advisor} hears it went great.

choices.label: Say you can't this time
choices.text: The lecture is canceled. The class gets a free hour and seems thrilled.

advisor.title: My Star Student
text: At the {venue} reception in {city}, {advisor} introduces you to a famous researcher as "my star student". The famous researcher turns to you, expectantly.

choices.label: Pitch your work in one minute

success.text: They ask one sharp question, then for your paper. You've made a real contact.

failure.text: You say "basically" eleven times. They are very kind about it.

choices.label: Ask about their work instead
choices.text: They talk for twenty minutes. You learn a lot and are remembered as a great listener.

choices.label: Laugh: "Star is generous."
choices.text: Everyone laughs, and {advisor} looks proud.

advisor.title: You're Running Reading Group
text: "{player} will run reading group this semester," {advisor} announces. This is the first you've heard of it.

choices.label: Run it properly
choices.text: You pick good papers and bring snacks, and attendance doubles.

success.text: Everyone takes a week, so you only present twice.

failure.text: Nobody signs up. You present for six weeks straight.

choices.label: Pick only papers for your project
choices.text: Every paper is about your project. The lab learns a lot about it, and so do you.

advisor.title: Weekly Progress Reports
text: {advisor} wants a written progress report every week from now on. "Just a few bullet points. Every Friday."

choices.label: Write them every Friday
choices.text: Writing down what you did turns out to be useful. Writing down what you didn't do, less so.

choices.label: Turn your notes into the report

success.text: Your lab notebook becomes the report, and it takes ten minutes a week.

failure.text: Your notes say "fixed thing" four times. {advisor} asks which thing.

choices.label: Propose a shared progress doc
choices.text: {advisor} likes it. Nobody reads it but you, which helps more than you expect.

advisor.title: A Very Motivated Undergrad
text: {advisor} asks you to mentor {mentee}, a new undergrad who is "very motivated". {mentee} has already emailed you twice.

choices.label: Give them a real subproject
choices.text: You write {mentee} a two-page plan. Explaining your project makes you understand it better.

choices.label: Start them on reading
choices.text: You send {mentee} five papers. They read all five by Tuesday and come back with good questions.

success.text: {labmate} is delighted. They've wanted a mentee for months.

failure.text: {labmate} is swamped, so {mentee} becomes yours anyway, a week late.

advisor.title: One Inspiring Keynote
text: {advisor} comes back from one inspiring keynote and wants {project} to go in a whole new direction. "Everything is about this now."

choices.label: Pivot {project}
choices.text: You're back at the idea stage, with half your novelty and a clean whiteboard.

choices.label: Add one experiment in that direction
choices.text: One small experiment satisfies the keynote energy, and it actually adds something.

success.text: A week later, {advisor} has moved on to a different keynote.

failure.text: A week later, they've watched the keynote twice more and are disappointed in you.

advisor.title: Caught in the Middle
text: {advisor} wants {project} framed as a methods paper. Your collaborator wants a findings paper. Both email you, separately, within the same minute.

choices.label: Side with your advisor
choices.text: Methods it is. The collaborator goes quiet for a week.

choices.label: Side with the collaborator
choices.text: Findings it is. {advisor} agrees, slowly, and remembers.

choices.label: Draft both framings
choices.text: You write two introductions. Everyone picks the second one, which neither of them proposed.

choices.label: Get them both on one call

success.text: Twenty minutes later they agree, and each thinks it was their idea.

failure.text: The call runs an hour. You leave with three framings instead of two.

advisor.title: "sounds good"
text: You send {advisor} a 2,000-word email laying out three options, with pros and cons for each. They reply "sounds good".

choices.label: Pick the option you liked
choices.text: You go with option B. Nobody objects, possibly because nobody read option A.

success.text: They call you, and you get ten genuinely useful minutes.

failure.text: They reply "sounds good" again.

choices.label: Send a three-line version
choices.text: The three-line version gets a real answer in four minutes.

advisor.title: Comments on Version 2
text: {advisor} finally sends comments on your draft of {project}. They are on version 2, and you are on version 5.

choices.label: Map their comments onto v5
choices.text: Half the comments are already fixed. The other half are good.

choices.label: Reply "Fixed in v5!"
choices.text: "Oh, great." You suspect v5 will be read sometime around v8.

choices.label: Ask them to read v5 now

success.text: They read v5 that night. The comments are sharp and on time.

failure.text: "Will do!" They do not.

advisor.title: Sabbatical Abroad
text: {advisor} is taking a sabbatical abroad for the next few months. "Nothing changes! We'll just meet at 6 am your time."

choices.label: Set three alarms
choices.text: You buy a second coffee maker. The first 6 am meeting goes fine, mostly.

success.text: {advisor} agrees: a written update each week, plus one call a month.

failure.text: "Let's try 6 am first and see." You set your alarm.

choices.label: Say 6 am is your best hour
choices.text: You're sharpest at dawn anyway. {advisor} is impressed by how awake you are.

choices.label: Stay up until 6 am instead
choices.text: For you, 6 am is the end of the day. The meetings are oddly relaxed.

advisor.title: The 6 am Call
text: You join the call at 5:58 am. {advisor} is eating lunch in the sun and wants to tell you about their host lab.

choices.label: Join their lab's meeting too
choices.text: You present to a lab you've never met, at dawn. Two of them email you afterward.

choices.label: Keep it to your project
choices.text: You get exactly the feedback you need, then sleep for another hour.

choices.label: Ask to visit for a week

success.text: "Yes! I'll find the travel money." You start looking at flights.

failure.text: "I'd love that, but the budget is tight this year."

advisor.title: A Week Abroad
text: You spend a week in {advisor}'s host lab abroad. The coffee is better, and so is the whiteboard.

choices.label: Give a talk to their lab

success.text: The questions are great and lunch runs long. They invite you to come back.

failure.text: The projector fights you for ten minutes. The discussion after is still good.

choices.label: Work side by side with {advisor}
choices.text: With real daytime meetings, you get more done in a week than in the last two months.

choices.label: Explore the city on the weekend
choices.text: You eat everything and come home with two ideas and a fridge magnet.

advisor.title: Back From Sabbatical
text: {advisor} is back from sabbatical, full of ideas, with a small souvenir for everyone. Your meetings return to a human hour.

choices.label: Pitch an idea from the trip

success.text: One idea sticks. {advisor} wants a paper on it.

failure.text: "Interesting! Let's revisit." It is never revisited.

choices.label: Enjoy your first 10 am meeting
choices.text: You sleep until 8, like a person.

choices.label: Ask for the people they met
choices.text: You get forty minutes of stories and three introductions to people you should know.

advisor.title: By Friday?
text: {advisor} asks if you could put together slides about your project for a funder visit, by Friday.
{advisor} needs two paragraphs on your project for a grant renewal. "Nothing fancy. By Friday?"

choices.label: Drop everything and do it well
choices.text: Your slides make it into the meeting, and your advisor mentions your name twice.

choices.label: Do a quick version
choices.text: It's good enough. Your advisor polishes it at midnight and doesn't mention it.

choices.label: Ask for until next Wednesday
choices.text: "Sure, Wednesday works." You could have just asked all along.

advisor.title: Would You Come With Me?
text: {advisor} closes the office door. Another university has made them an offer, a big one. "Nothing is decided. But if I go, would you come with me?"

choices.label: Say you'd come with them
choices.text: {advisor} looks relieved. That night you look up rents in a city you've never visited.

choices.label: Say you'd rather stay here
choices.text: "That's fair. We'd make it work either way." You tell your roommate you're not going anywhere.

choices.label: Ask for a few weeks to think
choices.text: "Of course." You think about it on the bus and through two entire seminars.

advisor.title: The Counteroffer
text: The department makes {advisor} a counteroffer. For two weeks the lab reads every closed door like tea leaves. Then {advisor} asks what you honestly think.

choices.label: Tell them to take the offer
choices.text: "Thank you. That helps more than you know." They accept the new job the next morning.

success.text: They stay. The counteroffer comes with a bigger lab, and they say your answer tipped it.

failure.text: "I hear you. I still think I have to go." They take the offer, and promise you won't be left behind.

advisor.title: Moving Week
text: You follow {advisor} to their new university, where you get a new badge and an empty lab that echoes.

choices.label: Set up the new lab yourself
choices.text: You label every machine and get every login working. {advisor} introduces you as the lab's co-founder.

choices.label: Meet the new department
choices.text: After twelve coffees in five days, you know who has the good GPUs and who has the good snacks.

choices.label: Live out of boxes and keep working
choices.text: Your desk is a box, and so is your chair. Your experiments don't notice the move, but your back does.

advisor.title: Advising From Afar
text: {advisor} moves to their new university, and you stay. Your meetings are on video now, and a professor down the hall agrees to sign your forms.

choices.label: Set a fixed weekly video call
choices.text: You meet Thursdays at 10, with an agenda sent the night before. It works better than the hallway chats ever did.

choices.label: Ask the local professor to co-advise

success.text: They say yes. Now you get twice the comments, and someone nearby when {advisor} is hard to reach.

failure.text: They're happy to sign forms, and only forms. You'll make the video calls work.

choices.label: Enjoy the quiet
choices.text: Nobody drops by your desk unannounced anymore. You get a lot done, and you and {advisor} drift a little.

career.title: Invert a Binary Tree
text: Your internship interview at {company} is for a research role on language models. The first question: "Let's warm up. Invert a binary tree."

success.text: You write six clean lines and handle the edge cases. The interviewer relaxes and asks about your research.

failure.text: You invert it twice, which gives back the original tree. The interviewer says "interesting" and writes something down.

success.text: Your questions turn it into a conversation. You solve it slowly, but they like how you think.

failure.text: You ask so many questions that time runs out before you write any code.

choices.label: Solve it fast, then pivot to research
choices.text: You solve it and steer the talk to your paper, while the interviewer glances at the clock.

career.title: Your Mentor Has Left the Building
text: In week two of your internship at {company}, your mentor announces they are moving to another team, effective Friday. Your project doc still says "TBD with mentor".

success.text: A senior researcher two desks over adopts you, and turns out to be better at this than your first mentor.

failure.text: Everyone is "happy to chat", but nobody is happy to mentor. You spend a week in limbo.

choices.label: Scope the project yourself
choices.text: You write your own project plan, and your manager approves it without reading it.

choices.label: Ask your old mentor for weekly chats
choices.text: They agree to a 30-minute call every Thursday from their new team.

career.title: Footnote 3
text: Your internship project at {company} ships. The press release thanks "the team". Your name is in footnote 3, spelled correctly.

choices.label: Add it to your CV
choices.text: "Shipped to millions of users." It is one line on your CV, and recruiters read that line first.

success.text: Your manager says they were about to bring it up. A return offer is on the table.

failure.text: "Let's revisit after headcount planning." Nobody knows when that is.

choices.label: Pitch a paper on the project

success.text: Legal approves a short workshop paper. People start citing it before you're back on campus.

failure.text: Legal says the paper can come out "after the next product cycle", which could mean next year.

career.title: Fellowship!
text: The fellowship is yours. For a whole year you don't have to TA or grade, and your calendar suddenly has room in it.

choices.label: Put the time into a bold idea
choices.text: You start the project you have been too busy to start, knowing it might not work.

choices.label: Catch up on sleep first
choices.text: You sleep properly for two weeks and are sharper than you have been since orientation.

choices.label: Celebrate with the lab
choices.text: You buy the lab dinner. {labmate} toasts "to no grading". A few labmates look envious.

career.title: Fellowship Feedback
text: The fellowship results are out, and you didn't get it. The reviewer comments come too. One says "too ambitious", another "not ambitious enough", and a third calls it "incremental".

choices.label: Look for the useful critique
choices.text: Two comments are actually useful. You fold them into next year's research statement.

choices.label: Vent to your cohort over dinner
choices.text: Half your cohort got the same three comments. Dinner turns into a dramatic reading.

choices.label: Start next year's application today
choices.text: You open a new document while you're still annoyed. It is a surprisingly productive mood.

career.title: Sixty Cover Letters
text: It's faculty application season, and each of 60 openings wants a custom cover letter plus two statements. You have already mixed up two department names.

choices.label: Write 60 truly custom letters
choices.text: Each letter names the faculty you would work with. It takes three weeks and part of your soul.

choices.label: Use one template plus a custom paragraph
choices.text: The letters are good and go out on time. You triple-check every department name.

choices.label: Apply only to your best 25
choices.text: You put more care into fewer letters, and your stress level survives application season.

career.title: Letter Pending
text: Three application portals show the same red status: "Letter of recommendation: not received." The deadlines were yesterday. The missing letter is from {advisor}.

success.text: {advisor} apologizes and uploads all three within the hour. Two committees say late letters are fine.

failure.text: {advisor} replies "on it!" and uploads one. The other two arrive next week.

choices.label: Send a page of talking points
choices.text: You send a one-page summary of your work. {advisor} uses it, and the letters go out the next morning.

choices.label: Email the search committees yourself
choices.text: Two of the three committees reply kindly. The third portal has no contact address, only a FAQ.

career.title: Equity and a Ping-Pong Table
text: A startup founder messages you: "We'd love you as a founding researcher. Generous equity, a ping-pong table, free snacks." The word "salary" does not appear.

choices.label: Hear them out
choices.text: The pitch is wild and a little convincing. You add startups to your search, just in case.

success.text: They name a real number: below big tech, above what you feared. You are more interested than you expected.

failure.text: "We think about compensation holistically." The conversation ends there.

choices.label: Decline and stay on your track
choices.text: You wish them luck. They thank you and ask if you know anyone else.

career.title: Wait, I Applied There?
text: A job-talk invitation arrives from a school you had completely forgotten you applied to. You search your sent mail to see what you promised them.

choices.label: Accept and study the department
choices.text: You read every faculty page and three of their papers. On the visit, you sound like you've wanted this job for years.

choices.label: Accept and give your usual talk

success.text: Your usual talk lands just as well. The search chair calls it "refreshingly clear".

failure.text: Your talk mentions collaborating with a research center they closed years ago.

choices.label: Decline politely
choices.text: You trade a flight for a free weekend. After a small pang, you feel relieved.

career.title: Twelve One-on-Ones
text: Campus visit: breakfast with the search chair, twelve 30-minute one-on-ones, your job talk, then dinner. Every single person asks, "So, tell me about your research."

choices.label: Be fully on for all twelve
choices.text: You give twelve slightly different versions of your pitch, and everyone loves you. You fall asleep in your dinner clothes.

success.text: You've read their papers and ask sharp questions. Half the meetings run over, happily.

failure.text: You mix up two professors' papers. One of them is very gracious about it.

choices.label: Save your energy for the talk
choices.text: You keep the one-on-ones short and give a sharp job talk. Dinner is quiet, but fine.

career.title: One Week Apart
text: One place wants your answer by next Friday. The place you like more will decide a week after that. Both say, "Take all the time you need."

choices.label: Ask the first place for more time

success.text: They give you two extra weeks. Now the dates line up.

failure.text: "We can't extend, but we really hope you'll join!" You still have until Friday.

choices.label: Ask the second place to decide sooner

success.text: Your email is polite and clear. They move their decision up by a week.

failure.text: They say they will "try", and then they don't.

choices.label: Ask {advisor} what they would do
choices.text: {advisor} tells you which one they would pick and, more usefully, why. You feel calmer about either.

career.title: A Famous Lab Writes Back
text: The head of a famous lab emails: they liked your talk and might have a postdoc opening. Could you chat on Thursday? Your heart rate disagrees with your calendar.

choices.label: Take the call and prepare hard
choices.text: You read their last ten papers. The call runs long and ends with "let's stay in touch". From them, that means something.

success.text: {advisor} knows them well and makes a call of their own. You go into Thursday with an ally.

failure.text: {advisor} says, "They work their postdocs very hard." That is all they say.

choices.label: Keep it as a plan B
choices.text: You reply warmly and keep it in your back pocket while you focus on your main search.

career.title: Employee #4
text: {labmate} pulls you aside: they are leaving to start a company, they just raised a small seed round, and they want you as employee number four. "You'd own a real piece of it."

choices.label: Say you're interested
choices.text: {labmate} is thrilled. You agree to talk details once you're on the job market.

choices.label: Ask to see the numbers first

success.text: The plan makes sense. {labmate} respects the questions and keeps a spot open for you.

failure.text: The plan is one slide with a hockey-stick curve on it. You say you'll think about it.

choices.label: Decline, but offer to advise
choices.text: You'll review their model evaluations for free. {labmate} is a little disappointed, but grateful.

career.title: A Starter Allocation
text: On day one at {company}, you get a GPU quota bigger than everything your lab has used in five years. The onboarding doc calls it "a starter allocation".

choices.label: Run every ablation you ever dreamed of
choices.text: You launch two hundred runs by Friday and learn more about scaling in a week than in two years of queueing.

choices.label: Plan runs as if GPUs were scarce
choices.text: Your mentor is impressed by how little compute you waste, and slightly confused by it.

choices.label: Send the lab a screenshot
choices.text: The lab chat goes quiet for a long minute. Then {labmate} replies with one crying emoji.

career.title: Pending Legal Review
text: Your internship paper at {company} is finished, but legal review flagged "possible product implications". The next review slot is in eleven weeks.

choices.label: Cut anything that sounds like a product
choices.text: Every product name becomes "a deployed system". Legal approves a thinner, vaguer paper, and it's out.

success.text: Your manager knows someone in legal. The paper clears in a week, untouched.

failure.text: The escalation lands in the same queue, one slot lower.

choices.label: Let it wait and enjoy the summer
choices.text: The paper goes into a folder called "someday". Your weekends come back for the rest of the internship.

career.title: Perfect Timing
text: Days before your proposal, the company you interned at emails a full-time offer, with a deadline. Your slides are 60% done. The salary section is 100% done.

choices.label: Ask them to wait until after

success.text: They give you a month. You go back to slide 23 calmer than you expected.

legion.title: A Power Analysis for the Pilot

legion.title: Ten Seeds and a Test
