text: Your discussion section lists 11 design implications. {advisor} reads it and leaves one comment: "Three. Readers remember three."

choices.label: Keep the three strongest
choices.text: Eight implications move to a file called later.md. The section is short and sharp.

success.text: All eleven ideas fit under three themes. Your advisor replies: "Yes."

failure.text: The three themes are called "Design", "More design" and "Other".

success.text: Five, with one sentence each. Your advisor agrees that five is also a number.

failure.text: You leave the meeting with three, and a comment about "focus".

research.title: 98% Agreement
text: You switched on model-suggested labels to speed up annotation. It worked: your annotators accept the suggestion {roll:96-99}% of the time, including the wrong ones.

choices.label: Add a no-suggestion condition
choices.text: Half the annotators label without help. It's slower, but now you can measure how much the suggestions steer them.

choices.label: Make it a paper of its own

success.text: It's a whole second paper about annotators trusting the model. You add it to the list, happily.

failure.text: Someone wrote that paper last year, and it's good, which somehow makes it worse.

choices.label: Hide suggestions until they choose
choices.text: Annotators label first, then see the model's guess. Speed drops, and so does the copying.

research.title: [NAME] Will Return in [NAME]
text: Your de-identification tool removes every name from the clinical notes, along with every "May", "Will" and "Hope". "Pt will return in May" now reads "Pt [NAME] return in [NAME]".

success.text: Forty rules later, May is a month again and will is a verb. The real names still go.

failure.text: Your rules fix "May" and miss a real name. You catch it in review, and start over, more carefully.

choices.label: Try another tool
choices.text: The second tool is careful with months, and also removes every number.

choices.label: Write up what de-identification breaks
choices.text: A short workshop paper on [NAME] and other casualties. Clinical NLP people love it.

research.title: pt
text: In your clinical notes, "pt" means patient, physical therapy, part-time and, once, "pint". Your model reads every one of them as patient.

choices.label: Build an abbreviation list with clinicians

success.text: Two clinicians sort 300 abbreviations in an afternoon and seem to enjoy it.

failure.text: They agree on 60% of them. Clinicians, it turns out, also guess.

choices.label: Let the model guess
choices.text: It guesses right most of the time. When it's wrong, it's confidently wrong.

choices.label: Make it an evaluation slice
choices.text: A new table: accuracy on ambiguous abbreviations. Your model's weak spot is now a contribution.

research.title: Lost in Evaluation
text: Your multilingual evaluation includes {roll:200-300} outputs in a language nobody in the lab reads. The automatic score says they're fine. You have no way to know.

choices.label: Recruit a native speaker
choices.text: A student from another department checks them for pizza. 30% are fluent nonsense.

choices.label: Use back-translation
choices.text: Back in English, they look fine. Back-translation is very forgiving.

choices.label: Read them yourself
choices.text: You read them over coffee. Most are fine, two are excellent, and one is a recipe.

research.title: Certainly!
text: Output 300 of 500. You notice you've started your emails with "Certainly!" and ended one with "I hope this helps!" It was to {advisor}.

choices.label: Take a break
choices.text: You take a walk and eat a sandwich, an hour away from all text. You come back sounding human.

choices.label: Sort the errors into categories
choices.text: Seven error types fit in one chart, and your analysis section gets much better. Output 301 is easier to read.

choices.label: Finish all 500 today
choices.text: Done by midnight. You dream in bullet points. Certainly!

research.title: A Paper That Doesn't Exist
text: Your model cites a paper that doesn't exist and credits it to {advisor}. The title sounds exactly like something {advisor} would write. You check twice.

choices.label: Add a citation check to your evaluation
choices.text: Every reference now gets checked against a real database, and 14% turn out to be invented.

success.text: Your advisor laughs, then asks, "Should I write it?" You're not sure they're joking.

failure.text: Your advisor frowns: "That's not even my area." Somehow that's the part that bothers them.

choices.label: Put it on a slide
choices.text: Your next lab-meeting talk opens with the fake paper. Everyone laughs, then three people check their own models.

research.title: Temperature Zero
text: You run the same prompt three times at temperature zero and get three different answers. Temperature zero, it turns out, is more of a mood.

choices.label: Run it five times, report the spread
choices.text: You report a mean and standard deviation over five runs. It costs five times as much, and it's honest.

success.text: Same input, same output, every time. You didn't know you'd missed that so much.

failure.text: The local model is perfectly consistent, and consistently worse. You switch back.

choices.label: Fix the seed and hope
choices.text: There is no seed setting. You add one to your config anyway, for morale.

research.title: Retry, Retry, Retry
text: You wake up to an email from billing. At 1 am your retry loop hit a rate limit, and retried, and retried. The lab's API budget for the month is gone.

success.text: "Thanks for telling me first. It happens." Your advisor moves some money around.

failure.text: A long pause, then: "Please write up what happened." You do, in great detail.

choices.label: Develop on a smaller model
choices.text: Development moves to a tiny model that costs almost nothing. This month's results are rougher.

choices.label: Write a budget guard
choices.text: You add a hard spending cap, an alert and a test for the retry loop. Nobody in the lab can do this again.

research.title: End of Life
text: {biglab} announces that the model your paper evaluates will be retired next month. Soon, nobody will be able to reproduce a single number in it.

choices.label: Rerun everything on its replacement
choices.text: A week of reruns shows the new model is better on average and worse on your examples, which is interesting.

choices.label: Release your saved outputs
choices.text: You archive and release every prompt and response, so anyone can check your work after the model is gone.

success.text: Open weights never change, so your results will reproduce long after you graduate.

failure.text: The open model needs more GPUs than your lab owns. You fall back to saving your outputs.

research.title: Graphic Content
text: The model refuses to summarize a clinical note about a sprained ankle, citing "graphic content". It refuses {roll:40-70} other notes too, mostly about knees.

choices.label: Reword the prompt
choices.text: "You are a helpful clinical assistant." It works for the ankle. The knees remain controversial.

choices.label: Use an open model
choices.text: The open model never refuses and makes more mistakes. You trade one problem for a more measurable one.

success.text: You make a table of refusal rates by body part. It's absurd, and everyone screenshots it.

failure.text: Refusal rates are already a well-known table. Yours is one more row.

research.title: 40 Regular Expressions
text: The model returns broken JSON {roll:2-4}% of the time. Your parser now has 40 regular expressions, and one of them is just a long sigh.

success.text: Valid JSON every time. You delete 40 regular expressions in one glorious commit.

failure.text: Constrained decoding works, slowly. Your evaluation now takes three days.

choices.label: Retry until it's valid
choices.text: Every bad output gets another try. It works, and the API bill grows a little every night.

choices.label: Count failures as errors
choices.text: Broken JSON counts as wrong. Your scores drop a point, and nobody can say you hid anything.

research.title: Shorter, Please
text: Your human raters prefer the baseline. You read their comments: "shorter", "shorter", "got to the point", "shorter".

choices.label: Control for length
choices.text: With length-matched pairs and a second round of ratings, your system wins, by a little, fairly.

choices.label: Report it as a finding
choices.text: "Raters prefer brevity" isn't new, but your data shows exactly how much.

success.text: Your system now says the same thing in half the words. The raters love it.

failure.text: Shorter, and now it leaves out the important part. The raters still prefer the baseline.

research.title: Cell 212
text: Your best result came from a notebook with 400 cells, run out of order over three weeks. Cell 212 depends on cell 388. You don't remember why.

choices.label: Rewrite it as a clean script
choices.text: After a day of untangling, the script runs top to bottom, and the result holds, minus half a point.

choices.label: Rerun it top to bottom and hope

success.text: It runs and gives the same number. You vow never to touch that notebook again.

failure.text: Cell 17 throws an error that cell 388 was hiding. The best result is gone.

choices.label: Report the result you can reproduce
choices.text: The number you can reproduce is two points lower. It goes in the paper, and you stop worrying about cell 212.

research.title: 4 GB
text: You accidentally commit a 4 GB model checkpoint to the lab repo. Every labmate's next pull takes an hour. The lab chat has noticed.

success.text: One careful force-push removes the checkpoint from history without losing anyone's work. The lab chat calls you a legend.

failure.text: The rewrite works, and also eats {labmate}'s last two commits. They're recoverable, eventually.

choices.label: Apologize in the lab chat, with donuts
choices.text: A dozen donuts and a sincere message. The pull still takes an hour, but now it comes with donuts.

success.text: {senior} fixes it in four minutes and admits the same thing happened to them in their first year.

failure.text: {senior} fixes it, then tells the story at every lab meeting for a month.

reviews.title: Well Written. Score: 2.
text: Reviewer 3: "The paper is well written, well motivated, and the experiments are thorough." Overall score: 2.
One review praises your writing for a full paragraph, then gives {paper} a 2.

choices.label: Ask what would change their mind

success.text: Your question is short and polite. The reviewer admits they "expected more" and raises the score half a point.

failure.text: Your question gets no answer. The 2 stays a 2, mysterious and well written.

choices.label: Flag the mismatch to the area chair

success.text: The area chair agrees that the review's text doesn't support its score, and weighs it less.

failure.text: The area chair reads your note as a complaint about a low score, which, to be fair, it is.

choices.label: Spend your effort on the others
choices.text: You thank Reviewer 3 for the kind words and answer the other two carefully.

reviews.title: One Line Over
text: A week after you submit, the program chairs write: {paper} runs one line onto page 9, past the 8-page limit, so it is desk-rejected.

success.text: On a second look, the stray line is part of the Limitations section, which doesn't count. The chairs reinstate the paper and apologize.

failure.text: The chairs reply, kindly and firmly, that the limit is the limit. You now know exactly how many lines fit on page 8.

choices.label: Tell the lab the whole story
choices.text: The lab laughs with you, mostly. Two labmates go back to their desks and count their own pages.

choices.label: Fix it and move on
choices.text: Two lines gone in five minutes, and a sticky note on your monitor: "COUNT THE PAGES." The paper waits for the next cycle.

reviews.title: Thanks, Everyone
text: Rereading the submitted PDF, you reach the last page. The acknowledgments, which you meant to delete, thank your lab by name and list your grant number.

success.text: The chairs thank you for reporting it and let the paper through without the paragraph.

failure.text: The chairs thank you for your honesty and desk-reject the paper, since the policy has no honesty clause.

choices.label: Ask your advisor what to do

success.text: Your advisor replies in four minutes: "Tell the chairs. Now." You do, and they let it through.

failure.text: Your advisor is on a long flight. By the time they land, the chairs have found it and desk-rejected the paper.

choices.label: Hope nobody reads acknowledgments
choices.text: You close the PDF. Surely nobody reads the acknowledgments. You check your email a lot this week.

reviews.title: Someone Read the Acknowledgments
text: An email from the program chairs: they read the acknowledgments. {paper} is desk-rejected for breaking anonymity.

choices.label: Start a pre-submission checklist
choices.text: Item one: delete the acknowledgments. Item two: check item one.

choices.label: Warn the lab
choices.text: Three labmates open their own drafts and delete the acknowledgments. You may have saved someone else's paper.

reviews.title: [TODO]
text: Scrolling the submitted PDF, you find it on page 6, in red: "[TODO: rerun with new seeds - {labmate}]". That's a real name in an anonymous submission, and the portal closes in nine minutes.

success.text: The new PDF lands with 40 seconds to spare. Your heart rate takes longer to recover.

failure.text: The upload finishes at 12:00:07, and the portal keeps the old PDF. A week later, the paper is desk-rejected.

success.text: The chairs accept a corrected PDF. They've seen worse, they say, and they list some.

failure.text: The chairs are sympathetic and firm. The name was visible to reviewers, so the paper is desk-rejected.

reviews.title: Accepted, Mid-Slide
text: Halfway through lab meeting, while {labmate} presents, your phone lights up: "{venue} decision: Accept."

choices.label: Wait until {labmate} finishes
choices.text: You sit on the news for 25 minutes. When you share it at the end, the room cheers, and {labmate} cheers loudest.

choices.label: Announce it right now
choices.text: The room cheers. {labmate}'s ablation slide never quite recovers.

choices.label: Slide your phone to {advisor}
choices.text: {advisor} reads it and keeps a straight face for nine more minutes before announcing it to the room.

reviews.title: Score Raised
text: In the final reviews, Reviewer 3 has raised their score from 2.5 to 3.5, enough to tip the decision: "The new analysis addresses my concern."

choices.label: Write down what convinced them
choices.text: Their concern was right, and fixing it made the paper better. You save the note for next time.

choices.label: Screenshot it for the lab chat
choices.text: The lab chat fills with celebration emoji. {labmate} asks to see your response, for science.

choices.label: Move the analysis into the main text
choices.text: The new analysis becomes Figure 4. Readers will find it, and so will citations.

reviews.title: Promises, Promises
text: The camera-ready is due in two weeks. Your rebuttal promised a new baseline, an error analysis, and a clearer Figure 2.

choices.label: Deliver every promise
choices.text: Everything you promised is in. Reviewer 2 will never check. You did it anyway, and your advisor noticed.

choices.label: Deliver the main ones
choices.text: The baseline and the figure make it in. The error analysis becomes "future work".

choices.label: Submit it as accepted
choices.text: Nobody stops you. Your advisor notices the missing error analysis and says nothing, which is worse.

reviews.title: Fourth Time
text: {paper} has been rejected so many times it has its own folder of reviews. This time, all three reviews are positive. One calls it "timely".

choices.label: Frame the acceptance email
choices.text: It goes on the wall by your desk, above a sticky note that says "resubmit".

choices.label: Reread the first round of reviews
choices.text: Round one said the paper wasn't ready, and round one was right. It's a much better paper now.

choices.label: Thank everyone who read all four
choices.text: Your advisor and {labmate} have read every version. You buy the first round, and they make you tell the whole story.

reviews.title: Nominated
text: The acceptance comes with a Best Paper nomination. For two months you rehearse a 30-second thank-you. At the ceremony, another paper wins.

choices.label: Clap, sincerely
choices.text: The winning paper is very good. You clap, and someone behind you whispers that yours was their favorite.

choices.label: Add "nominee" to your CV
choices.text: "Best Paper Nominee" goes on your CV, and you will argue with anyone who says it doesn't count.

choices.label: Read the winner on the flight home
choices.text: It's excellent. You fill two pages with ideas, and only one of them is "why not us".

reviews.title: Outstanding Paper
text: A second email from the chairs, two weeks after the acceptance: {paper} has been selected for an Outstanding Paper Award at {venue}.

choices.label: Read it five times, then call home
choices.text: Your family doesn't know what the award is. They are prouder than anyone at the conference will be.

choices.label: Rebuild the talk from scratch
choices.text: An award paper gets a full room. You rewrite the talk for it, and it's the best one you've ever given.

choices.label: Post the news
choices.text: Your post is shared by people you've only ever cited. Your inbox fills with invitations and one recruiter.

reviews.title: 4, 4, and 2
text: Scores: 4, 4 and 2. The meta-review summarizes the 2, quotes the 2, and recommends rejection.

choices.label: Write to the senior area chair

success.text: A thoughtful reply: the meta-review "could have engaged more with the positive reviews." The decision stands, but you feel heard.

failure.text: A template reply thanks you for your feedback on the review process.

choices.label: Reread the 2 for anything real
choices.text: Under the tone, one point is real. You fix it, and the next version is harder to reject.

choices.label: Resubmit next cycle, same paper
choices.text: You send the same paper to new reviewers and hope for two 4s and a quiet third.

reviews.title: Read by Nobody
text: You wrote a careful response with two new experiments. Not one reviewer replied, and the meta-review repeats the concerns you answered.

choices.label: Put the new experiments in the paper
choices.text: The rebuttal experiments go into the next version. This time, someone has to read them.

success.text: The chairs agree that the reviewers didn't engage and make a note of it. Nothing changes, but you feel better.

failure.text: An auto-reply, then nothing. You have now written two documents nobody read.

choices.label: Close the laptop for the evening
choices.text: You call a friend over for dinner and don't open the reviews again until Monday.

reviews.title: In Light of the Other Reviews
text: Reviewer 1 had given a 3.5. After reading Reviewer 2, they lowered it to 2.5: "I agree with R2's concerns." You had answered R2's concerns.

success.text: The area chair acknowledges the score change was never explained. The decision stands, but the note goes on record.

failure.text: Your report is filed. So, apparently, is everything else.

choices.label: Fix R2's concern anyway
choices.text: Annoyingly, the fix makes the paper better. R2 was rude, but not entirely wrong.

choices.label: Vent to {labmate}
choices.text: {labmate} once had a reviewer lower a score twice. You feel better, and slightly worse about science.

choices.label: Shrug it off like a veteran
choices.text: Three rejections ago, this would have ruined your week. Today it ruins an afternoon, at most.

reviews.title: Decision at Dinner
text: Your phone buzzes halfway through dinner with your family. It's the {venue} decision, and it's a no. Everyone has already seen your face.

choices.label: Tell them what happened
choices.text: Nobody at the table knows what a meta-review is. They are outraged on your behalf anyway, and it helps.

choices.label: "Just work stuff."
choices.text: Nobody believes you. You skip dessert and reread the reviews under the table.

choices.label: Explain peer review, in full
choices.text: Twenty minutes later, your uncle has a theory about Reviewer 2, and it's annoyingly plausible.

reviews.title: Revise and Resubmit
text: {venue} says Revise and Resubmit. The reviewers' list of changes would rewrite half of {paper}, and the revision is due right after the holidays.

choices.label: Rewrite half the paper
choices.text: By the end you have a new framing and a new analysis. It's nearly a new paper, and a better one.

choices.label: Fix only the must-fix list
choices.text: You make the required changes and politely explain the rest in the response letter.

success.text: {labmate} takes the related work and the discussion, and somehow the paper still reads like one person wrote it.

failure.text: {labmate}'s half is good, but in a completely different voice. The paper now has two personalities.

reviews.title: Ten Papers, Two Weeks
text: An area chair asks you to review ten papers. Reviews are due in two weeks.
Reviewing assignments are out: ten papers in two weeks. One of them is 40 pages with appendices.

choices.label: Review all ten, properly
choices.text: You write ten careful reviews. The area chair remembers your name, and you learn more about why papers get rejected than your own rejections ever taught you.

choices.label: Take three, decline seven
choices.text: You send three thorough reviews on time, and the area chair thanks you for saying no early.

choices.label: Accept all ten and skim
choices.text: Your reviews are short, and the area chair notices. Somewhere, you've just become someone's Reviewer 2.

reviews.title: Would You Be Willing to Review?
text: A journal editor writes: "Would you be willing to review this manuscript? We'd appreciate your comments within 21 days." It's 48 pages.
Your advisor forwards a review request with one line: "You'd be great for this." It's due in three weeks.

choices.label: Accept and do it properly
choices.text: It takes three evenings, and you come out of it with a lot of respect for clear figures.

choices.label: Accept, then forget until the reminder
choices.text: You write it in one panicked night, after the second reminder.

choices.label: Decline politely
choices.text: You suggest a labmate instead. The editor thanks you for the quick reply.

reviews.title: Slight Delay
text: Reviews for {paper} were due Monday. A banner on the portal says "slight delay". By Thursday your lab refreshes it in shifts, and at 1 am they appear.

choices.label: Read them right now
choices.text: You read every word at 1 am and start the response by 2, with a headache.

choices.label: Sleep first, read with coffee
choices.text: Seven more hours of not knowing. The reviews are the same in the morning, and you're kinder to them.

success.text: {labmate} sends a summary: "Two fair, one weird, all fixable."

failure.text: {labmate}'s summary is one word long: "oof".

reviews.title: Welcome Back, Reviewer
text: Reviewer 2's review of {paper} opens with the same sentence as last cycle's Reviewer 3, typo included.

choices.label: Show them you fixed what they asked

success.text: You go through their old concerns point by point, each one fixed. You can almost hear them nod.

failure.text: They've moved on. This cycle's concerns are all new, and you spent your response on the old ones.

choices.label: Treat it as a fresh review
choices.text: You answer it like any other. They don't need to know that you know.

choices.label: Tell the AC it's a repeat reviewer

success.text: The area chair reads the old and new reviews side by side and notices how much the paper has changed.

failure.text: The area chair replies, correctly, that reviewers are allowed to review a paper twice.

reviews.title: Confidence: 5
text: Reviewer 3's review of {paper} is three sentences long, with a score of 1 and confidence 5. The third sentence is "Not convincing."

choices.label: Ask the AC to weigh it lightly

success.text: The area chair agrees that three sentences can't carry a 1, and says so in the meta-review.

failure.text: The area chair replies that confidence 5 means confidence 5.

choices.label: Answer it like a full review
choices.text: Three sentences get three careful answers. Nobody will ever read that review as closely as you just did.

choices.label: Spend the rebuttal on the other two
choices.text: You thank Reviewer 3 in one line and give your best work to the reviewers who gave theirs.

reviews.title: More, Please. Fewer, Please.
text: Reviewer 1: "Too many experiments; the main story gets lost." Reviewer 3: "More experiments are needed." Both are about Section 5 of {paper}.

success.text: You side with the reviewer the area chair seems to agree with. It shows in the meta-review.

failure.text: You side with the reviewer the area chair didn't. The other reviewer notices, too.

success.text: You move some experiments to the appendix, so both reviewers can read it as a win.

failure.text: Your middle ground pleases neither. Both reply "partially addressed".

choices.label: Let the area chair sort it out
choices.text: One neutral line points out the contradiction. Settling it is the area chair's job, and sometimes they do it.

reviews.title: Compare With Yourself
text: Reviewer 2 asks why {paper} doesn't compare against a paper from last year. That paper is yours. The review is anonymous, so you can't just say "that's us".

choices.label: Compare to it, politely
choices.text: You run your old method as a baseline, written up in the third person, and it loses gracefully.

choices.label: Flag it confidentially to the AC

success.text: The area chair sees the problem at once and tells Reviewer 2 the comparison is already in the paper, in spirit.

failure.text: The area chair writes back: "Please address the reviewer's concern in your response."

choices.label: Add the citation and sigh
choices.text: Reviewer 2 asked you to cite yourself, so you do. Your citation count goes up by one.

reviews.title: The Fourth Review
text: Two days into the rebuttal period, a fourth review of {paper} appears, marked "emergency". It's the shortest of the four, and the harshest.

choices.label: Answer it first
choices.text: It gets your best paragraph, right at the top. The other three get slightly shorter answers.

success.text: You add one neutral sentence about the timing, and the area chair weighs the late review accordingly.

failure.text: The note reads as a complaint. The area chair weighs it accordingly.

choices.label: Treat it like the others
choices.text: All four reviews get calm answers. The late one doesn't get to set the tone.

reviews.title: 2,500 Characters
text: The rebuttal limit is 2,500 characters. Your draft reply to Reviewer 2 alone is 6,000.

choices.label: Cut to your three strongest points

success.text: Each point is one claim and one number. It's the best thing you've written all month.

failure.text: You cut the numbers and keep the adjectives.

choices.label: Write it like a telegram
choices.text: "Baseline added STOP Table 3 fixed STOP thank you STOP". It fits. The reviewers may not find it as funny as you do.

choices.label: Answer only Reviewer 2
choices.text: Reviewer 2 gets 2,500 careful characters. Reviewers 1 and 3 get nothing, and they may notice.

reviews.title: Where's the Control?
text: Reviewer 1 likes {paper} but wants a control condition. Without one, they can't tell whether your tool helped or your participants were just being nice.

success.text: You explain why a formative study doesn't need a control, with two citations. Reviewer 1 accepts it.

failure.text: Your defense is correct and a little defensive. Reviewer 1 is unmoved.

choices.label: Promise it as future work
choices.text: You add a paragraph to the limitations and a promise to the response. Reviewers have heard it before, but it helps a little.

choices.label: Run a quick online version in five days
choices.text: Forty online participants and five short nights later, your tool beats the control. Your body files a complaint.

reviews.title: Have You Considered LLMs?
text: Reviewer 3's main suggestion: "The authors should consider using large language models." {paper} is entirely about large language models. It says so in the title.

success.text: "As the title suggests, our work uses large language models throughout." It's polite and only slightly smug.

failure.text: It reads more pointed than you meant. Reviewer 3 does not reply.

choices.label: List Sections 1 through 6
choices.text: You list every section that uses one, with page numbers. It feels great, and the area chair can tell.

choices.label: Laugh, then answer it as a real question
choices.text: Maybe they meant a different kind of model. You add a second model family, and the paper is better for it.

reviews.title: A Different Paper
text: Reviewer 2's summary of {paper} describes a method you didn't propose, tested on a dataset you didn't use. The weaknesses are about that paper, too.

choices.label: Correct the summary gently
choices.text: One kind paragraph explains what the paper actually does. Whether Reviewer 2 reads it is up to Reviewer 2.

success.text: The area chair compares the summary to your abstract and sets the review aside.

failure.text: The area chair is on vacation. Their backup is also on vacation.

choices.label: Answer it as if they'd read it
choices.text: You answer the concerns that could apply to your paper and skip the rest, which is oddly relaxing.

reviews.title: Could Go Either Way
text: All three reviews of {paper} give borderline scores, and all three say "I could go either way."

choices.label: Write your strongest rebuttal
choices.text: You answer every concern with numbers and leave nothing on the table except your sleep.

choices.label: Keep it short and polite
choices.text: You write five pleasant lines per reviewer. Borderline papers sometimes tip on tone.

choices.label: Write it off and aim higher next cycle
choices.text: You send a minimal response and start a list for the next version. It's a relief to stop hoping.

reviews.title: Rebuttal, Room 1214
text: The rebuttal window for {paper} opens on the first morning of a conference you're attending, and it closes five days later.

choices.label: Write it in the hotel at night
choices.text: You go to talks by day and write by night on hotel coffee. The response is good, and you look like the hotel coffee.

choices.label: Skip a day of sessions
choices.text: You spend a day in your room with the rebuttal and miss the keynote everyone talks about at dinner.

success.text: {labmate}, at home and rested, takes two reviewers. You answer the third between sessions.

failure.text: {labmate} is at the same conference. You write it together in the hotel lobby at midnight.

reviews.title: The Experiment, a Day Late
text: At 6 am the morning after you submit {paper}, you wake up knowing the one experiment that would have made it airtight.

choices.label: Run it now, for the rebuttal
choices.text: By the time reviews arrive, the result is in a table, ready to paste. The post-deadline rest never happens.

choices.label: Save it for the next paper
choices.text: It goes in a file called next_paper.md. The file is getting long, which is a good sign.

choices.label: Write it down and go back to sleep
choices.text: You write it on a sticky note and sleep until noon, the best sleep since the deadline.

reviews.title: Findings Counts
text: {paper} is in {venue}, not the main conference. {advisor} and {labmate} both tell you Findings is a real publication, several times each.

choices.label: Call it a win and mean it
choices.text: You update your CV and sleep well for the first time in a month.

choices.label: Ask whether Findings gets a poster

success.text: It does, in a shared session. Three people stop by, and one of them becomes a collaborator.

failure.text: Findings is virtual-only this year. You present to a poster board of avatars.

choices.label: Start the main-track follow-up now
choices.text: You open a new document called "main track, for real".

reviews.title: The Paper You Reviewed
text: Decisions are out. {paper} is rejected, and the paper you gave a 2 as a reviewer for {venue} is accepted.

choices.label: Read their camera-ready
choices.text: They fixed everything you asked for. It's a good paper now, partly thanks to you, and you're not sure how to feel about that.

choices.label: Tell {labmate}, without saying which
choices.text: {labmate} guesses the paper in four seconds. You neither confirm nor deny, and you both feel better.

choices.label: Close the tab and get ice cream
choices.text: Peer review is a lottery, and this week you bought a ticket for someone else.

reviews.title: The One-Line Meta-Review
text: The meta-review for {paper} is one sentence long: "The reviewers raised several concerns." It does not say which.

choices.label: Reread the reviews for clues
choices.text: Two concerns show up in more than one review. That's probably the sentence the area chair meant to write.

success.text: The area chair replies with a real paragraph and an apology. It's the most useful part of the whole review.

failure.text: The reply is also one sentence long.

choices.label: Print it and pin it to the wall
choices.text: It goes up next to {labmate}'s "Thank you for your submission."

reviews.title: A Great Workshop Paper
text: The meta-review for {paper}: "Not ready for {venue}, but this would make a great workshop paper." It's meant kindly, and it still stings.

choices.label: Send a short version to a workshop
choices.text: You send four non-archival pages. A few people hear about the work now, and the full paper stays free for a main venue.

choices.label: Hold out for another main venue
choices.text: You fix the core concerns and aim high again. They said "not ready", not "not good".

choices.label: Split it into two papers
choices.text: You cut it in two and keep the stronger half for now. It's clearer than the whole was, and a little smaller.

reviews.title: Next Deadline: Three Weeks
text: An hour after the rejection, {advisor} writes: "Let's turn {paper} around for the next deadline. It's in three weeks."

choices.label: Turn it around fast
choices.text: For three weeks you do nothing else, and most concerns get answered. Sunlight becomes a rumor.

choices.label: Ask for one more cycle to fix it

success.text: "Fair. Better a strong paper later than a tired one now." The fixes go deeper than the reviews asked.

failure.text: "Three weeks is plenty." It isn't, but now you know the plan.

choices.label: Fix only the top two concerns
choices.text: You fix two concerns properly and acknowledge the rest, which fits in three weeks.

reviews.title: Mostly Fair
text: A week later, you reread the reviews of {paper} with fresh eyes. Annoyingly, they're mostly fair.

choices.label: Turn them into a fix list
choices.text: You end up with eleven items, sorted by effort, which is much easier to look at than a rejection.

choices.label: Stay a little mad
choices.text: You get a lot done this week, and you type very loudly.

choices.label: Write one thank-you line in your notes
choices.text: "Thanks, Reviewer 1, for the error analysis idea." Nobody will read it, and you feel better anyway.

reviews.title: Was It Wasted?
text: You have to tell your clinical collaborators that {paper} was rejected. Their first question: "So was the study wasted?"

success.text: They follow the whole process, luck included. One says it sounds like grant review, only faster.

failure.text: They follow along until "Reviewer 1 lowered the score after reading Reviewer 2", then look worried for you.

choices.label: Share the kind parts of the reviews
choices.text: Every reviewer praised the clinical setting. You read them those lines and keep the rest for the lab.

choices.label: Invite them to plan the resubmission
choices.text: They bring a better scenario and two ideas you'd never have had. It costs a meeting a week, and the next version is stronger.

reviews.title: Cited, Rejected
text: {paper} is rejected from {venue} on Tuesday. On Thursday, its arXiv version is cited twice. One of the citing papers calls it "seminal".

choices.label: Let it make you feel better
choices.text: Three reviewers said no, and two papers have cited it since. You decide the papers count more.

choices.label: Update arXiv with the fixes
choices.text: Version 2 goes up with the reviewers' fixes in it. It's the one people will cite from now on.

choices.label: Screenshot it for {advisor}
choices.text: {advisor} replies with three exclamation marks, the most you've ever received.

reviews.title: It's a Lottery Anyway
text: {labmate}, your co-author on {paper}, wants to resubmit it unchanged: "It's a lottery anyway. New reviewers, new numbers."

choices.label: Agree and buy another ticket
choices.text: You resubmit it with very little work. It is also exactly the paper three people just rejected.

choices.label: Insist on fixing the concerns
choices.text: {labmate} sighs and takes the related work. The new version is better, and you're both a bit tired of each other.

choices.label: Fix the two cheapest things
choices.text: You fix Figure 2 and add one missing citation. It's slightly better than a lottery ticket.

reviews.title: Their First Rejection
text: {paper} was {mentee}'s first paper; their name is second on it. They haven't seen the decision yet. You have to tell them.

choices.label: Tell them in person, with cookies
choices.text: {mentee} takes it well, eats three cookies and asks what to fix first.

choices.label: Forward the reviews with a long note
choices.text: Your note says which comments matter and which are noise. {mentee} saves it in a folder called "how this works".

choices.label: Ask {advisor} to tell them
choices.text: {advisor} handles it kindly. {mentee} wonders, a little, why it wasn't you.

reviews.title: Add It. Now Remove It.
text: The new reviewers want Section 5 removed from {paper}. Last cycle's reviewers asked you to add Section 5. It took three weeks.

choices.label: Remove it
choices.text: It took three weeks to write and three seconds to delete. The paper is tighter, and a little less convincing.

success.text: Two sentences at the top of Section 5 say why it's there. Nobody will ask again, from either side.

failure.text: Your explanation ends up longer than the section. You trim both and lose an afternoon.

choices.label: Move it to the appendix
choices.text: Section 5 lives on in Appendix C, where the people who want it can find it and nobody else has to.

reviews.title: Too HCI, Too NLP
text: Last cycle, reviewers called {paper} "too HCI for this venue". This cycle, with nearly the same text, it's "too NLP for this venue".

choices.label: Rewrite it for one community
choices.text: You pick a side and cut what the other side loved. It hurts, and it reads better.

choices.label: Aim for an interdisciplinary venue
choices.text: You read a year of papers from a venue built for exactly this. Reviewers there might call it a bridge.

choices.label: Turn it into a position paper
choices.text: If nobody can tell which field it belongs to, maybe that's the argument. The paper gets bolder and easier to attack.

reviews.title: Many Happy Returns
text: On your birthday, at 9 am and before the cake, {venue} rejects {paper}.

choices.label: Cake first, reviews tomorrow
choices.text: You leave the laptop closed and have cake with your friends. The reviews will still be there tomorrow.

choices.label: Read them now
choices.text: You read all three over breakfast. You know exactly what to fix, and exactly how to ruin a birthday.

choices.label: Ask the lab never to mention it
choices.text: Nobody mentions it. {labmate} brings a cake that says "Happy Birthday" and, in very small letters, "R2 is wrong".

reviews.title: The New Reviewer
text: After a whole Revise and Resubmit, {paper} is rejected. The deciding review comes from someone who wasn't in the first round, with concerns nobody raised before.

success.text: The chairs explain that a first-round reviewer dropped out. They sound genuinely sorry, which helps a little.

failure.text: A polite reply says the process was followed. It was, and that's the problem.

choices.label: Take it to a journal
choices.text: A journal has room for the whole story, and reviewers who stay for every round. The paper gets longer, and calmer.

choices.label: Revise once more for the next cycle
choices.text: You answer the new concerns. The paper has now satisfied three sets of reviewers, at least on paper.

reviews.title: Emergency Reviewer Needed
text: At 9 pm, an area chair writes: a reviewer dropped out, so could you possibly review one paper by noon tomorrow? "It's short," they add. It's 14 pages.

choices.label: Say yes and do it properly
choices.text: You finish at 3 am. The area chair thanks you by name, which is the most an area chair can do.

choices.label: Say yes, keep it short
choices.text: You send a fair, short review at 11:58 am. Your best paragraph is about Figure 2.

choices.label: Decline kindly
choices.text: Someone else gets the email next. You sleep fine, mostly.

reviews.title: New Follower
text: A new follower on social media. Their latest post complains about "papers that ignore obvious baselines", in the exact words of the review that rejected your last paper.

choices.label: Follow back
choices.text: They like your next paper thread within a minute. You wonder whether they know it's you.

choices.label: Mute them
choices.text: Your feed is calmer, and you stop reading their posts for clues.

choices.label: Post a thread about your baselines

success.text: The thread does well, and they like it. You will never know if they noticed.

failure.text: The thread gets four likes. One is from them, which is somehow worse.

tasks.title: Every Author Reviews
text: This cycle, {venue} asks every author to review too. Right after you submit {paper}, five papers land in your queue, due in three weeks.

choices.label: Do all five properly
choices.text: Five careful reviews. You learn more about what makes a paper land than your own last three submissions taught you.

choices.label: Do them fast
choices.text: Five short reviews, on time. One is three sentences long. Somewhere, an area chair makes a note.

choices.label: Ask the chairs for a lighter load

success.text: The chairs cut you to two, since you're a student. You do both properly and keep your evenings.

failure.text: "Every author reviews five." Now you have five reviews and one slightly awkward email thread.

tasks.title: Could You Take a First Pass?
text: {advisor} forwards their own review assignment: "Could you take a first pass on these four?" The reviews are due in nine days.

choices.label: Write careful drafts
choices.text: Four careful drafts. {advisor} submits them almost unchanged and says you have a good eye.

choices.label: Send short notes
choices.text: Four sets of bullet points, done in an evening. {advisor} writes the reviews from them, with a small sigh.

choices.label: Ask to be listed as a sub-reviewer
choices.text: {advisor} adds your name. The conference thanks you by email, and two area chairs now know who you are.

tasks.title: Bidding Season
text: Reviewer bidding is open: {roll:1600-2000} abstracts, bids due Thursday. The site shows 25 at a time and logs you out every hour.

choices.label: Read titles for an evening
choices.text: An evening of titles. You bid on eight papers you'd actually like to read, and spot two suspiciously close to yours.

choices.label: Bid "eager" on everything in your topic
choices.text: Ten minutes of clicking. The system takes you at your word: you get your topic, and plenty of it.

choices.label: Skip bidding and accept your fate
choices.text: Your evening is free. Fate assigns you a 40-page theory paper and one about crop yields.

tasks.title: Too Short
text: The area chair writes: your review is "too short to help the authors". Could you expand it by Friday? It is four sentences. One is "The paper is fine."

choices.label: Rewrite it properly
choices.text: You reread the paper and write a real review. The area chair thanks you by name in the discussion.

choices.label: Add two paragraphs
choices.text: Two paragraphs of "the authors may wish to consider". It meets the length. The area chair replies "Thanks." with a period.

choices.label: Point out that the paper was short too
choices.text: The area chair does not find this funny. You're left off next year's reviewer list, which you decide is a win.

tasks.title: Three Pings
text: Discussion period. The area chair has pinged you three times about the authors' response. It is 2,400 words long and has its own table of contents.

choices.label: Read it and engage
choices.text: The response is good, so you drop two of your three concerns. For once, the discussion goes somewhere.

choices.label: Raise your score
choices.text: One click and the pings stop. You hope the response was as good as it was long.

choices.label: Reply "I maintain my score"
choices.text: Four words, sent. The area chair's next message to you is noticeably shorter than the first three.

tasks.title: Eight Months Later
text: A journal sends the revised version of a paper you reviewed eight months ago, with a 30-page response to reviewers. You remember none of it.

choices.label: Reread both versions
choices.text: A full day with both PDFs side by side. The revision is much better, and your second review says so in detail.

choices.label: Check only your old points
choices.text: All six of your points are answered, more or less. You recommend acceptance in an evening and feel only slightly guilty.

choices.label: Decline politely
choices.text: The editor replies within a minute. They'll find someone new, who will ask for everything you already asked for.

tasks.title: Question 3
text: Halfway through grading, you notice the answer key is wrong on question 3. You have already graded {roll:50-70} exams with it.

choices.label: Regrade everything
choices.text: You regrade every exam. Not one regrade request arrives, and the professor asks for you as TA next year.

choices.label: Accept both answers
choices.text: Everyone gets the points. The class average goes up, and so do the regrade requests on question 4.

choices.label: Tell the professor and let them decide
choices.text: The professor thanks you and drops question 3 entirely. You spend a long evening redoing every total.

tasks.title: Everyone Did 40%
text: Group peer evaluations are in. Every member of every group says they did 40% of the work. One group of four adds up to 160%.

choices.label: Read the commit histories
choices.text: A day in the git logs. They tell a clearer story, including one 3 am commit titled "fixed everyone's stuff".

choices.label: Give each group one grade
choices.text: Three students email to say it's unfair, and each of them is a little bit right.

choices.label: Meet the three most confusing groups
choices.text: Three meetings, three versions of every story. By the third, you could referee anything.

tasks.title: Hard but Fair
text: The professor asks you to write the midterm. "Just two questions. Hard but fair." The exam is in nine days.

choices.label: Write new questions
choices.text: Two new questions, each solved three ways. You understand the material better than when you took the course.

choices.label: Adapt last year's
choices.text: You change the numbers and the variable names. One student finishes in twelve minutes; their roommate took the course last year.

choices.label: Borrow from the textbook
choices.text: Done in an hour. Eleven students recognize problem 4.7, the average is 96%, and the professor asks you to write a makeup.

tasks.title: 8 am, Saturday
text: You're proctoring the 8 am Saturday final: 140 students in a silent gym for three hours, under a wall clock that runs four minutes fast.

choices.label: Proctor and grade in the room
choices.text: You grade forty exams between whispered questions about question 2. That's a day of grading you won't have to do later.

choices.label: Swap with another TA
choices.text: They take your Saturday. You take their Monday review session, and they've already told the students you're great.

choices.label: Bring coffee for the whole room
choices.text: You wheel in 140 coffees, and it's the calmest final you've ever seen. Several students write "thanks for the coffee" on their exams.

tasks.title: Moving Day
text: The course switches to a new website mid-semester. Someone has to move fourteen weeks of slides, quizzes and due dates. You are someone.

choices.label: Do it carefully
choices.text: It takes a full day of copying and checking. Every due date is right, and no student will ever notice.

choices.label: Move only what's due this month
choices.text: Done by dinner. Next month you'll do it again, with less memory of how.

success.text: Your script moves everything in eleven minutes. You spend the rest of the day showing it to people.

failure.text: The script moves everything and sets every due date to January 1, 1970. You fix them by hand.

tasks.title: As an AI Language Model
text: A student's essay begins with the words "As an AI language model". The rest is very confident and about a different book.

choices.label: Fill in the six-page integrity form
choices.text: The form takes six pages and a flowchart. The professor is impressed, and the office asks you to redo it on a newer template.

choices.label: Talk to the student first
choices.text: They turn red and rewrite it by Friday. The new essay is messier, and clearly theirs.

choices.label: Forward it to the professor
choices.text: The professor takes it from here, with a sigh you can hear through email.

tasks.title: A Letter From Their TA
text: A student from your section asks you for a recommendation letter for a summer research program. It's due in a week. You remember their name, and that they sat by the window.

choices.label: Write a warm, specific letter
choices.text: You dig up their assignments and office-hours questions. The letter is specific and kind, and in April they get in.

choices.label: Offer a short one
choices.text: Three honest sentences. They thank you politely and ask the professor too, just in case.

choices.label: Suggest they ask the professor
choices.text: They do. The professor agrees, then asks you for "a few notes on the student". You write the notes.

tasks.title: You're Up in an Hour
text: Today's lab meeting presenter cancels. {advisor} messages: "{player}, could you present instead?" Lab meeting is in an hour.

choices.label: Show your messy results honestly
choices.text: Half the plots have no axis labels. The lab spots a bug you'd have found in three weeks, and {advisor} likes the honesty.

choices.label: Present a paper you read last week
choices.text: You remember most of it. For the parts you don't, {labmate} jumps in, kindly.

choices.label: Run a brainstorm instead
choices.text: A wall of sticky notes produces one good idea. Nobody notices you prepared nothing, except {advisor}.

tasks.title: One Slide, Two Hours
text: The department open house for admitted students needs one slide about your research, in two hours. The required template is purple.

choices.label: Make one clean slide
choices.text: You use one figure and one sentence. It's the best slide you've ever made, and it takes the whole afternoon.

choices.label: Reuse your last title slide
choices.text: It shows your name and last year's date. An admitted student asks what your research is about, and the slide does not say.

choices.label: Use one striking figure, no words

success.text: Admitted students crowd around it, asking what it means. You explain it eleven times, happily.

failure.text: Admitted students crowd around it, asking what it means. So does {advisor}.

tasks.title: The Dean's Tour
text: The dean tours the building tomorrow, and {advisor} has promised a live demo of {project}. It has not run since Tuesday.

choices.label: Polish it tonight
choices.text: It runs, and the dean says "fascinating" twice. You got three hours of sleep.

choices.label: Record a backup video
choices.text: The live demo crashes in the first minute. The video plays perfectly, and the dean never knows.

choices.label: Show slides instead
choices.text: The dean nods politely and asks to see "the real thing" next time. {advisor} winces.

tasks.title: Your Two Buddies
text: The department assigns you two first-year "buddies". They message you about the cluster every day, often at the same time, about different errors.

choices.label: Hold a weekly Q&A
choices.text: Thursdays at 4, with snacks. By week three, first-years you've never met start showing up.

choices.label: Answer every message
choices.text: You reply within minutes, every time, and they adore you. Your own jobs sit in the queue, untouched.

choices.label: Point them to the docs
choices.text: There are no docs. They find this out on their own, and stop asking you anything, including to lunch.

tasks.title: The Eleventh Time
text: Eleven people asked you the same cluster question this month. Three of them were the same person.

choices.label: Write the onboarding doc
choices.text: It takes a full day and twelve screenshots. The questions stop, and the lab treats you like a hero.

choices.label: Record a ten-minute video
choices.text: Four takes. People watch it at double speed and still ask you, but less often.

choices.label: Pin your best Slack answer
choices.text: Nobody reads pinned messages. Questions twelve through fifteen arrive by Friday.

tasks.title: Only You Know
text: A new postdoc needs access to the data server, and only you know how the permissions work. You set them up two years ago, at night, and wrote nothing down.

choices.label: Walk them through it
choices.text: A day of user groups and one mysterious file called keys_old. They're in, and they owe you lunch.

choices.label: Write it down this time
choices.text: It takes longer than just doing it. But the next person won't need you, and neither will future you.

choices.label: Send them to IT
choices.text: IT opens a ticket. The ticket opens another ticket. The postdoc gets access in three weeks and remembers who sent them.

tasks.title: Three High Schoolers
text: A summer outreach program sends you three high schoolers for a week. They're thrilled to be here, and one of them has already read your paper.

choices.label: Give them a mini project
choices.text: By Friday they've built a tiny classifier and a slide deck with spinning transitions. You're prouder than you expected.

choices.label: Let them test your prototype
choices.text: They break it four new ways in one afternoon, which is free user testing.

choices.label: Show them lab life, snacks included
choices.text: You give them a tour and a lot of snacks. One of them decides grad school looks "chill", and you don't correct them.

tasks.title: A Photo of a Receipt
text: Your travel reimbursement is rejected. The receipt is a photo of a receipt, in another currency, partly covered by your thumb.

choices.label: Find the original
choices.text: You empty every bag you own and find it folded inside your boarding pass. Approved in a week.

choices.label: Fill in the "missing receipt" form
choices.text: The form is four pages long and includes a signed statement about a sandwich. Approved in six weeks.

choices.label: Let the $43 go
choices.text: No more forms. It's instant noodles for the rest of the week.

tasks.title: Eight Modules by Friday
text: The annual research-ethics refresher is due Friday: eight modules with quizzes, or your study approval is paused.

choices.label: Do it properly
choices.text: You get the certificate and learn two things you probably should have known already.

success.text: All eight quizzes passed at double speed. The narrator sounded like a chipmunk, but a well-informed one.

failure.text: You fail the module 6 quiz three times, then rewatch it twice at normal speed.

choices.label: Do it during lab meeting
choices.text: You pass all eight modules. {advisor} asks you a question twice and gets no answer either time.

tasks.title: In Ink
text: Your plan-of-study form needs {advisor}'s signature, in ink, by the 15th. {advisor} is traveling for the next two weeks.

choices.label: Mail it to their hotel
choices.text: It comes back signed, with a coffee ring and a doodle of the hotel pool. You refreshed the tracking page forty times.

choices.label: Ask the grad office about e-signatures

success.text: The office says e-signatures have been fine for years. Nobody told the form, but it's done in an hour.

failure.text: Three emails later: e-signatures are accepted on every form except this one.

choices.label: Wait for them to come back
choices.text: You file it two weeks late. The grad office sends a reminder with three exclamation marks and puts a hold on your registration.

tasks.title: Nobody's Monitors
text: Equipment inventory: every monitor in the lab needs a tag. You find three that belong to nobody, according to every list you check.

choices.label: Report them
choices.text: Two forms and a call with Facilities. The department thanks {advisor} for the lab's "exemplary" inventory.

choices.label: Adopt one as your second screen
choices.text: Papers on the left, code on the right. {labmate} had been eyeing that monitor for a year.

choices.label: Tag them to the lab and move on
choices.text: Three stickers later, the lab officially owns three monitors nobody can explain.

tasks.title: Your Plan Expires Friday
text: Your survey tool's subscription ends on Friday, in the middle of the study for {project}. The renewal email says "Act now!" in three colors.

choices.label: Pay out of pocket
choices.text: $240, and the study runs on. You file for reimbursement and try not to think about how that will go.

choices.label: Move to the university's free tool
choices.text: A day rebuilding every question in an interface from another decade. The data comes out in a slightly different format.

success.text: The department covers it from a fund nobody knew existed. You make a note of the fund.

failure.text: The reply arrives after the subscription ends. The study pauses for two weeks.

tasks.title: Forty Signatures
text: Finance needs a signed receipt for each of the 40 gift cards you gave participants in {project}. The participants are now all over the country.

choices.label: Email all 40
choices.text: Forty emails, then forty reminders. By Friday you have 34 signatures and six people who think it's a scam.

success.text: You build a two-minute form with a signature box, and 38 people sign within a day. You will reuse it forever.

failure.text: The form works, but its emails go straight to spam. You find out a week later.

choices.label: Ask for an exception
choices.text: Finance approves it, after a two-page memo and a meeting {advisor} has to attend. {advisor} is not thrilled.

tasks.title: Numbers You Never Tracked
text: The IRB's annual check-in for {project} is due in a week. It asks how many people you enrolled each month. You never tracked that.

choices.label: Rebuild them from your calendar
choices.text: A day with your calendar and old emails. The numbers are exact, and you find two sessions you forgot to analyze.

choices.label: Estimate honestly and say so
choices.text: "About 30, exact months unclear." The IRB accepts it, with a polite request to keep a log from now on.

choices.label: Ask for a week's extension
choices.text: Granted. The new due date lands in your busiest week, and the numbers are still untracked.

tasks.title: Approved Servers Only
text: A new data policy: all study data must move to the approved server by Friday. Yours lives on four machines, two drives and a laptop you stopped using.

choices.label: Move it carefully
choices.text: A day of copying and checking. For the first time since Year 1, all your data is in one place.

choices.label: Move it and hope the paths still work

success.text: Moved by noon, and every path still works. You don't trust it, but it works.

failure.text: Moved by noon. By Wednesday, every script you own fails with "file not found".

choices.label: Ask for an extension
choices.text: Granted, until the end of the month. The data office copies {advisor} on its reply.

tasks.title: You Know Your Work Best
text: {advisor} asks you to draft your own recommendation letter. "You know your work best." You have never once called yourself "exceptional".

choices.label: Write it honestly
choices.text: Your draft is accurate and a bit modest. {advisor} adds two sentences that make you blush.

choices.label: Write it boldly
choices.text: "Among the top 1% of students I have known." {advisor} tones it down to 5%, still the nicest thing anyone has said about you.

choices.label: Swap drafting duty with {labmate}
choices.text: You write theirs; they write yours. Both letters glow, and {advisor} notices they share every adjective.

tasks.title: A Supporting Note
text: {mentee} is applying to grad school and asks you for a "supporting note" that {advisor} can use in their letter. It's due in five days.

choices.label: Write a detailed note
choices.text: Two pages on everything {mentee} did. {advisor} uses half of it word for word.

choices.label: Send bullet points
choices.text: Five bullet points. {advisor} follows up with three questions, each in its own email.

choices.label: Help them ask {advisor} directly
choices.text: {mentee} asks {advisor} themselves, nervously. It's good practice, and you can tell they hoped you'd do it.

tasks.title: Three Signatures
text: The annual progress report needs a committee meeting and three signatures by the end of the month. Your committee has three calendars and no overlap.

choices.label: Get everyone in one room
choices.text: It takes eleven emails and a 7:30 am slot. The meeting turns out to be useful, and {committee} has a great idea for your next project.

choices.label: Collect signatures by email
choices.text: Three signatures in three weeks, plus one reply that just says "signed (where?)".

choices.label: Ask the grad office for more time
choices.text: They give you another month. The report moves onto next month's to-do list, and so does the dread.

tasks.title: Nine Goals
text: The progress report asks you to compare last year's goals with what happened. You set nine goals. You met two, and did seven other things.

choices.label: Report it straight
choices.text: Two met, seven changed, each with a reason. {advisor} appreciates the honesty and suggests fewer goals, chosen better.

choices.label: Turn the seven into a story

success.text: Read in order, the seven other things look like a plan. You almost believe it yourself.

failure.text: {committee} asks how goal 4 led to project 7. It didn't, and now everyone knows.

choices.label: Edit last year's goals to match
choices.text: Last year's goals now describe this year perfectly. {advisor} still has the original and says nothing.

tasks.title: Expected Graduation
text: A form asks for your expected graduation date. You and {advisor} fill in your parts separately, and write different years.

choices.label: Talk it through
choices.text: After an hour on the next two years, you leave with a plan and a date. Your heart beats a little faster.

choices.label: Use your advisor's year
choices.text: You write the later year. Now it's on an official form, which makes it feel very real.

choices.label: Write a range
choices.text: "Spring or fall, this year or next." The grad office accepts it. {advisor} raises an eyebrow.

tasks.title: Just a Few Calls
text: A friend from another lab asks you to co-organize a workshop at next year's conference. "It'll be fun! Just a few calls."

choices.label: Say yes
choices.text: It is many calls, plus a call for papers and a keynote speaker who replies once a month. Everyone learns your name.

choices.label: Offer to run just the website
choices.text: The site takes one evening. Your name goes on the organizer list anyway.

choices.label: Decline kindly
choices.text: Your friend understands and asks someone else. Next year you see the workshop on the program, a little wistfully.

tasks.title: By 5 pm
text: The university press office needs a quote about chatbots in hospitals by 5 pm. It's 3:40. They found you by searching the website for "chatbot".

choices.label: Write a careful two-sentence quote
choices.text: Forty minutes for two sentences. They print it with your name spelled right, and your aunt shares it with everyone.

choices.label: Pass it to {advisor}
choices.text: {advisor} gives the quote from a hallway at 4:55, slightly out of breath, and mentions "my student's work".

choices.label: Send them your abstract
choices.text: They print one sentence of it: "We leverage a novel multi-stage framework." Nobody learns what you do.

tasks.title: For Readability
text: A stranger opens a pull request on your paper's code. It rewrites everything "for readability": 212 files changed, every variable renamed.

choices.label: Review it line by line
choices.text: A day of diffs. Two of their changes really are better, so you keep those. They star the repo anyway.

success.text: Everything still runs, a little faster. You feel lucky and slightly uneasy.

failure.text: Everything breaks. Three issues titled "nothing works" arrive before lunch.

choices.label: Thank them and close it
choices.text: A polite note and one click. They reply with a long essay on code style. You don't read it.

tasks.title: The Reproducibility Badge
text: {venue} offers a reproducibility badge for {paper} if its code runs in a container by next week. Right now it runs on your laptop, on a good day.

choices.label: Containerize it
choices.text: After three days of dependency fights, it builds. The badge is small and orange, and you love it.

choices.label: Skip the badge
choices.text: No badge, and the week is yours. Months later, someone emails to ask whether the code runs. It does not.

choices.label: Ask {labmate} for help
choices.text: {labmate} knows containers and has it working in an afternoon. You owe them, and they've already named the favor.

tasks.title: In Plain Words
text: The proceedings want a 150-word plain-language summary of {paper}. Your first draft says "leverage" four times and "novel" twice.

choices.label: Write it properly
choices.text: Three drafts later, it says what you did and why it matters, with no leveraging at all. It may be the best paragraph you write this year.

choices.label: Ask a non-academic friend to read it
choices.text: Your friend reads it twice and asks, "So it's a chatbot?" You rewrite it around that question, and it's much better.

choices.label: Simplify the abstract and send it
choices.text: You delete every third word of the abstract. It's 150 words, and still only your reviewers could follow it.

tasks.title: Take 14
text: {venue} accepts an optional video figure for {project}. Your narration is on take 14. On take 13, the radiator joined in.

choices.label: Finish it properly
choices.text: Take 22 is the one, and it's under three minutes. Your work has never sounded this good.

choices.label: Record the screen, add captions
choices.text: The video is all captions and a slow, confident cursor. It's clear and only slightly eerie.

choices.label: Skip it
choices.text: It's optional. You close the recorder and go to sleep. Most papers don't have one either.

teaching.title: 120 Midterms
text: You have 120 midterms to grade by Monday. The stack on your desk is taller than your monitor.
The midterm stack arrives: 120 exams of six questions each, due back Monday morning.

choices.label: Grade all weekend
choices.text: You finish at midnight on Sunday, and now you dream about partial credit.

choices.label: Write a rubric first, then batch it

success.text: The rubric takes an hour and saves ten. Question by question, you finish Saturday night.

failure.text: Halfway through, an answer breaks your rubric. You regrade 60 exams.

choices.label: Spread it across the week
choices.text: You grade for two hours every evening. Grades go in Wednesday, and the professor sends one pointed email.

teaching.title: Half a Point
text: A student requests a regrade on a half-point question. The request is 900 words long and cites the syllabus, two lecture slides and the student handbook.

choices.label: Give them the half point
choices.text: The student is thrilled. By evening, four more requests arrive, each citing "precedent".

success.text: They reply, "Fair enough, thanks!"

failure.text: They escalate to the professor, with your email attached and highlighted.

choices.label: Forward it to the professor
choices.text: The professor gives them the half point and CCs you.

teaching.title: The Line Goes Out the Door
text: It's office hours the day before the assignment is due, and the line goes out the door. Everyone has the same bug.

choices.label: Stay until everyone is helped
choices.text: You leave at 9 pm, after thirty-one students with the same off-by-one error. You could fix it in your sleep, and soon will.

choices.label: Explain the bug once, to everyone

success.text: One explanation at the whiteboard sends thirty students away happy.

failure.text: Half the room follows. The other half lines up again, now with two bugs.

choices.label: Post a fix on the forum, end on time
choices.text: Your forum post gets 40 thank-yous and one complaint that you posted it too late.

teaching.title: A Very Good Question
text: At office hours, a student asks why the chatbot from lecture sounds so sure when it is wrong. Nobody has a good answer, which might make it a paper.

choices.label: Write the idea down right away
choices.text: It goes into your ideas file, with the student's question word for word.

choices.label: Talk it through with the student
choices.text: Forty minutes later you have a whiteboard full of ideas, and office hours have run over.

success.text: {advisor} lights up: "That's a real gap." It goes on the list for next semester.

failure.text: {advisor} points you to three papers that already did it. At least now you've read them.

teaching.title: You're Teaching Tomorrow
text: The professor has a cold and emails at 8 pm: "Could you give tomorrow's lecture? Slides attached." There are 74 slides. You have seen about ten of them.

choices.label: Present their slides as they are
choices.text: You get through it. On slide 52 you learn something new, live, along with everyone else.

choices.label: Stay up and make the slides your own
choices.text: You cut it to 40 slides and add two examples from your research. Three students stay after to ask about it.

choices.label: Turn it into a discussion class

success.text: You give each small group one question and walk the room. Students call it the best class of the semester.

failure.text: "Discuss in groups" becomes 70 students on their phones. You present the slides after all.

teaching.title: The Autograder Is Down
text: The night before the assignment is due, the autograder starts failing every submission, including the reference solution. The forum has 63 new posts.

success.text: A dependency updated itself. You pin the version at 1 am and the forum calms down.

failure.text: By 4 am it passes the reference solution and fails everything else. You go to bed anyway.

choices.label: Ask the professor for an extension
choices.text: The deadline moves 48 hours. The forum celebrates as if you personally saved them.

choices.label: Grade by hand next week
choices.text: Everyone submits on time. Next week, you run 90 programs one by one.

teaching.title: Is the Deadline Tonight?
text: A student email arrives at 3:04 am: "Is the deadline tonight?" The deadline was at midnight. You know the email arrived at 3:04 because you are awake too.

choices.label: Reply right now
choices.text: "It was at midnight, but submit now and I'll ask the professor." They submit at 3:09, and you're asleep by 4.

choices.label: Reply kindly in the morning
choices.text: You close the laptop and reply at 9 am. The student had already submitted at 3:10.

choices.label: Ask yourself why you're awake at 3 am
choices.text: You go to bed, and your sleep schedule thanks you, a little.

choices.label: Reply, then keep writing until 5
choices.text: Since you're up anyway, you also finish a section of your paper.

teaching.title: Very Patient, Talks Too Fast
text: Your TA evaluations are in. Nearly every comment says the same thing: "Very patient, talks too fast." One student just wrote "fast".

choices.label: Practice talking slower
choices.text: You record yourself and time it. It's painful to watch, and your next practice talk goes better.

choices.label: Focus on the "very patient" part
choices.text: You print it and stick it above your desk.

choices.label: Ask {labmate} to time your next talk

success.text: {labmate} raises a hand every time you speed up. By the end you're both laughing, and you're slower.

failure.text: {labmate} forgets to show up. You talk fast to an empty room.

teaching.title: Old Nemesis
text: You are assigned to TA the course you barely passed as an undergrad, the one with the proof-heavy final. This time, you grade that final.

choices.label: Relearn it properly this time
choices.text: On your second pass through the textbook, it finally clicks. Your undergrad self would be stunned.

choices.label: Stay one lecture ahead
choices.text: You learn each topic the night before you teach it. It works, mostly, and nobody notices.

success.text: Office hours fill up. Students say you explain it best, because you remember why it's hard.

failure.text: A student asks, "So... should we trust your grading?"

teaching.title: Years Later
text: An email from a student you TA'd years ago: they are an engineer now, and your office hours are why they stayed in computer science. They remember your name. You remember their bug.

choices.label: Write back properly
choices.text: You write a long, warm reply. It's the best thing you've written all month, and nobody will review it.

choices.label: Invite them to talk to your students
choices.text: They give a guest talk to this year's class. Two students ask them for internship referrals.

choices.label: Save it in a "good days" folder
choices.text: You start a folder for emails like this. The next rejection stings a little less.

teaching.title: The Grading Pile
text: The midterms are in: 140 of them, due back by Monday. The professor is at a conference.
All 38 final projects arrive at 11:59 pm, and some have videos.

choices.label: Grade them all carefully
choices.text: Every one gets fair, detailed feedback. Two students email to say thank you, which almost never happens.

choices.label: Make a rubric and move fast
choices.text: The rubric is a work of art. The grading goes fast, and nobody complains.

choices.label: Ask the other TA to split it
choices.text: They say yes, and you owe them one.

travel.title: After the Conference
text: You finally get a visa appointment for your conference trip. It's nine days after the conference ends.
The consulate's earliest open slot is the week after your conference. The booking site suggests you "plan ahead".

choices.label: Refresh the booking site every hour

success.text: At 2:47 am a cancellation appears. You book it before anyone else wakes up.

failure.text: No earlier slot opens in time. You'll give your talk over video, from your desk.

success.text: The letter works. The consulate moves your appointment up by three weeks.

failure.text: The consulate thanks your advisor for the letter and changes nothing. The talk goes remote.

choices.label: Plan a remote talk now
choices.text: You record a clean talk and keep your week. The hallway chats will have to wait.

travel.title: Lost Luggage
text: Your suitcase is somewhere between two airports. Your talk at {venue} is tomorrow morning, and you're wearing the hoodie you slept in on the plane.

success.text: Nobody looks at your clothes. They look at your results, and two people ask for your slides.

failure.text: You spend the first minute apologizing for the hoodie. The talk recovers, mostly.

choices.label: Buy an outfit in {city} tonight
choices.text: The only open store sells souvenir shirts. Everyone remembers the talk in the I LOVE {city} shirt.

choices.label: Wait at the airport for the bag
choices.text: The bag arrives at 11 pm. You get four hours of sleep and a clean shirt.

travel.title: The Keynote Nap
text: Jet lag hits during the keynote. You wake up to applause and a slide that just says "Thank you!"
You close your eyes for one second during the keynote. When you open them, it's the Q&A.

choices.label: Ask your neighbor for a summary
choices.text: They sum it up in two sentences. You trade emails, and it turns out you only needed the two sentences.

choices.label: Go back to the hotel and sleep
choices.text: You sleep 14 hours. You miss the afternoon sessions and wake up a person again.

choices.label: Drink a third coffee
choices.text: You make it through the poster session wide awake. At 3 am you are still wide awake.

travel.title: Behind the Pillar
text: Your poster board for {paper} is behind a concrete pillar. In the first half hour, one person stops by, and they are looking for the restroom.

choices.label: Stand in the aisle and wave people in

success.text: You pull in a steady stream. Someone says it's the best poster they've ever seen behind a pillar.

failure.text: People nod politely and keep walking. Your arm gets a good workout.

choices.label: Ask the organizers to move you

success.text: They move you next to the coffee urn, the best spot in the hall.

failure.text: "All boards are final." The pillar and you will spend the afternoon together.

choices.label: Tape a QR code to the pillar
choices.text: Almost nobody visits, but your paper gets a few dozen downloads that afternoon.

travel.title: Your Hero, at Your Poster
text: Your research hero walks up to your poster for {paper}, reads it for a full minute, and asks the one question you hoped nobody would ask.

choices.label: Admit the limitation, say what's next
choices.text: They nod. "That's the right next step." You will replay this moment for years.

success.text: They smile. "Fair point. Send me the paper." You send it before they reach the next poster.

failure.text: They say "Hm," and move on. You're still glad they stopped.

choices.label: Freeze, then ask for a selfie
choices.text: The question goes unanswered, but the selfie is excellent.

travel.title: Your Poster, Explained
text: A visitor stops at your poster and explains {paper} to you, confidently and incorrectly, for six minutes.

success.text: They pause, then say, "Oh, that's even better." You trade emails.

failure.text: They nod, then repeat their version a little louder.

choices.label: Nod and take notes
choices.text: Half of what they said is wrong. The other half is a decent idea for future work.

choices.label: Hand them a printed copy
choices.text: They take the paper and keep explaining it, now while pointing at it.

travel.title: The Seat Next to Yours
text: At the networking dinner in {city}, the name card next to yours belongs to the author of your favorite paper.

choices.label: Ask about their paper
choices.text: They light up. Nobody has asked about that paper in years, and you get the story behind Table 3.
